items.t: Practice makes perfect.
items.d: Things get easier the more you try them.

items.t: Look before you leap.
items.d: Think about what could happen before you act.

items.t: Two heads are better than one.
items.d: A friend might spot an answer you missed.

items.t: Many hands make light work.
items.d: Tidying a room is easier when everyone helps.

items.t: Better late than never.
items.d: You can still make a start, even if you meant to start sooner.

items.t: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
items.d: Wait to see what happens before you count on it.

items.t: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
items.d: Keep another plan ready in case your first one fails.

items.t: Actions speak louder than words.
items.d: Helping someone means more than just saying you will.

items.t: Every cloud has a silver lining.
items.d: Even a hard day can hold something good.

items.t: A stitch in time saves nine.
items.d: Fix a small tear now, before it gets bigger.

items.t: Haste makes waste.
items.d: When you rush, mistakes can make you do the job twice.

items.t: Out of sight, out of mind.
items.d: It's easy to forget things you don't see often.

items.t: Easy come, easy go.
items.d: Things gained quickly can disappear quickly, too.

items.t: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
items.d: A shared job can get messy when everyone tries to be in charge.

items.t: All that glitters is not gold.
items.d: Something can look fine without being as good as it seems.

items.t: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
items.d: Big jobs start small. Just take the first step.

items.t: With enough work, an iron rod can be ground into a needle.
items.d: Keep going and you can do things that seem impossible.

items.t: Sharpening the knife does not delay cutting the wood.
items.d: Getting ready well first makes the real job faster.

items.t: Hearing a hundred times is not as good as seeing once.
items.d: Seeing something yourself teaches you more than being told.

items.t: When you drink the water, remember who dug the well.
items.d: Say thank you to the people who helped you get what you have.

items.t: Three people walking together always have something to learn from each other.
items.d: Everyone knows something you don't, so you can learn from anyone.

items.t: One generation plants the trees, and the next gets the shade.
items.d: Good things you do today can help people long after.

items.t: Don't wait until you are thirsty to dig a well.
items.d: Get ready ahead of time instead of waiting until you need it.

items.t: A fall into a pit is a gain in your wit.
items.d: When you make a mistake, you get smarter for next time.

items.t: Fall down seven times, get up eight.
items.d: Failing is okay. What counts is that you keep getting back up.

items.t: Even monkeys fall from trees.
items.d: Even experts make mistakes, so don't feel bad about yours.

items.t: A frog in a well does not know the great ocean.
items.d: There is a big world outside what you know. Be curious about it.

items.t: Ten people, ten colors.
items.d: Everyone is different and likes different things, and that is good.

items.t: Even dust, when piled up, becomes a mountain.
items.d: Tiny steps every day add up to something big.

items.t: Even a stone becomes warm if you sit on it for three years.
items.d: Patience and sticking with it get results in the end.

items.t: If you are in a hurry, go the long way around.
items.d: A safe, careful way often gets you there faster than rushing.

items.t: Fortune comes to the house that laughs.
items.d: Happy, cheerful people tend to have good things come their way.

items.t: See how others act, and fix your own ways.
items.d: Notice good and bad examples, and learn from them yourself.

items.t: Haraka haraka haina baraka. Hurry, hurry has no blessing.
items.d: Rushing often spoils things. Take your time and do it well.

items.t: Pole pole ndio mwendo. Slowly, slowly is the way to go.
items.d: Steady, careful steps get you where you want to go.

items.t: Haba na haba hujaza kibaba. Little by little fills the pot.
items.d: Small bits, added up day by day, make something big.

items.t: To live a long time is to see many things.
items.d: The longer you live, the more you get to see.

items.t: A person is a person through other people.
items.d: We are shaped by our family and friends, and we need each other.

items.t: When spider webs unite, they can tie up a lion.
items.d: Small people working together can do big things.

items.t: Rain does not fall on one roof alone.
items.d: Good times and hard times touch everyone, so we should help each other.

items.t: Wisdom is like a baobab tree: no one person can wrap their arms around it.
items.d: Nobody knows everything, so we all share what we know.

items.t: Knowledge makes a person humble.
items.d: The more you learn, the more you see how much is left to learn.

items.t: One and one together can make eleven.
items.d: Two people working together can be much stronger than two alone.

items.t: Do good, and good will come back to you.
items.d: Being kind to others often makes others kind to you.

items.t: What you have learned is a handful. What you have not learned is the whole world.
items.d: There is always more to learn, so keep being curious.

items.t: Patience is the key to relief.
items.d: Waiting calmly often helps problems get solved.

items.t: The dogs bark, but the caravan moves on.
items.d: Keep going with your goal, even if some people say unkind things.

items.t: Learning when you are young is like carving in stone.
items.d: What you learn as a child stays with you for a long time.

items.t: No bad thing comes without some good.
items.d: Even a tough thing can turn out to teach you something nice.

items.t: Face bad weather with a good face.
items.d: Smile through tough days and they feel easier.

items.t: Little by little, you go far.
items.d: Slow, regular steps can take you a long way.

items.t: Tell me who you walk with, and I'll tell you who you are.
items.d: The friends you choose can change how you act, so choose kind ones.

items.t: Whoever keeps at it will reach the goal.
items.d: Keep trying and you will reach your goal.

items.t: The shrimp that falls asleep is carried off by the current.
items.d: If you stop paying attention or trying, things can pass you by.

items.t: Nobody is born knowing.
items.d: Everyone learns step by step, so it's fine to ask and try.

items.t: Measure seven times, cut once.
items.d: Check your work carefully before you do something you can't undo.

items.t: Patience and hard work will grind everything down.
items.d: Keep working steadily and even hard things get done.

items.t: Without work, you can't even pull a fish out of a pond.
items.d: Nice things usually take some effort.

items.t: Morning is wiser than evening.
items.d: A problem often seems easier after a good night's sleep.

items.t: A word is not a sparrow: once it flies out, you can't catch it.
items.d: Think before you speak, because words can't be taken back.

items.t: Better to have a hundred friends than a hundred rubles.
items.d: Friends are worth more than money.

items.t: The eyes are afraid, but the hands do it.
items.d: A big job looks hard at first, but once you start, you can do it.

items.t: Repetition is the mother of learning.
items.d: Doing something again and again helps it stick in your mind.

items.t: A good laugh and a long sleep are the best cures.
items.d: Having fun and resting well help you feel better.

items.t: People live in each other's shelter.
items.d: We all need and help one another.

items.t: Praise the young and they will flourish.
items.d: Kind encouragement helps children grow and try harder.

items.t: Better a wee bush than no shelter.
items.d: A small help is still better than nothing.

items.t: He who goes slowly goes safely and goes far.
items.d: Taking your time keeps you safe and gets you far.

items.t: He who sleeps catches no fish.
items.d: You have to be awake and active to get what you want.

items.t: Whoever finds a friend finds a treasure.
items.d: A good friend is worth more than gold.

items.t: Rome wasn't built in a day.
items.d: Great things take a long time, so be patient.

items.t: Every beginning is hard.
items.d: Starting something new feels tricky, but it gets easier.

items.t: The morning hour has gold in its mouth.
items.d: Early in the day is a good time to get things done.

items.t: Trying beats studying.
items.d: Reading about something helps, but trying it teaches the most.

items.t: No effort, no prize.
items.d: Good things come to those who work for them.

items.t: Shared sorrow is half a sorrow.
items.d: Telling a friend about a problem makes it feel lighter.

items.t: Even if the sky falls, there is a way out.
items.d: There is always a way through a tough problem.

items.t: Kind words you give come back kind.
items.d: Speak nicely to others and they will speak nicely to you.

items.t: The small pepper is the hotter one.
items.d: Small people can be strong and clever.

items.t: Starting is half the job.
items.d: Once you begin something, you are already halfway there.

items.t: A tree bends while it is young.
items.d: Good habits are easiest to learn when you are young.

items.t: One tree does not make a hill, but three trees together make a high mountain.
items.d: Working together, we can do more than alone.

items.t: If you have patience, you will have stew.
items.d: Waiting and sticking with a job brings a tasty reward.

items.t: Heavy and light loads are both carried together.
items.d: A team shares the hard jobs and the easy ones.

items.t: Not all knowledge is taught in one school.
items.d: You can learn from many people and places, not just one.

items.t: What is the most important thing in the world? It is people, it is people, it is people.
items.d: People matter more than things.

items.t: The sweet potato does not speak of its own sweetness.
items.d: Be humble. Let your good deeds speak for you.

items.t: Soft water on hard stone, it keeps hitting until it makes a hole.
items.d: Gentle but steady effort can beat even hard problems.

items.t: Little by little, the bird builds its nest.
items.d: Big things are built one small piece at a time.

items.t: Shared joy is double joy.
items.d: Good news feels even better when you share it.

items.t: He who would be a leader must be a bridge.
items.d: A good leader helps people connect and cross over.

items.t: There is no bad weather, only bad clothes.
items.d: With the right gear, you can enjoy any day outside.

items.t: The more languages you know, the more times you are a person.
items.d: Each language opens a new world of friends and ideas.

items.t: Make haste slowly.
items.d: Be quick but careful, because rushing causes mistakes.

items.t: Fortune favors the brave.
items.d: Trying something bold gives you a better chance of success.

items.t: Slow and steady wins the race.
items.d: Keep going at a steady pace and you can beat a faster but careless racer.

items.t: Great oaks from little acorns grow.
items.d: Big things start from tiny beginnings.

items.t: Birds of a feather flock together.
items.d: People who are alike tend to become friends.

items.t: The early bird catches the worm.
items.d: Getting started early gives you the best chance.

items.t: One never notices what has been done; one can only see what remains to be done.
items.d: Even when you work hard, you see what is left to do. Remember to notice how far you have come too!

items.t: We must have perseverance and above all confidence in ourselves.
items.d: Keep going when things are hard, and believe that you can do it.

items.t: I was taught that the way of progress was neither swift nor easy.
items.d: Getting better at something takes time and effort, and that is normal.

items.t: I am among those who think that science has great beauty.
items.d: Science is not just facts. Finding out how things work can feel as lovely as music or art.

items.t: I learned very early the difference between knowing the name of something and knowing something.
items.d: Knowing a bird's name is a start. Watching what it eats and how it flies is real knowing.

items.t: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.
items.d: Be honest with yourself, especially when you really want something to be true.

items.t: What I cannot create, I do not understand.
items.d: If you can build it or explain it yourself, you truly understand it.

items.t: I don't feel frightened by not knowing things.
items.d: It is fine not to know everything. Not knowing is where the fun of finding out begins.

items.t: We are a way for the cosmos to know itself.
items.d: We are made from the universe, and when we study the stars, the universe is learning about itself.

items.t: The cosmos is within us. We are made of star-stuff.
items.d: Many atoms in your body were made inside stars long ago.

items.t: If you wish to make an apple pie from scratch, you must first invent the universe.
items.d: Not every atom in a pie was made at the start. Stars made many of them later.

items.t: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.
items.d: If someone says something really amazing, ask for really good proof.

items.t: Imagination will often carry us to worlds that never were. But without it we go nowhere.
items.d: Dreaming up new ideas is the first step to every discovery.

items.t: A book is proof that humans are capable of working magic.
items.d: A book lets you hear the thoughts of someone you have never met, even from long ago.

items.t: Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us.
items.d: He was talking about a photo of Earth taken from far away, where our planet looks like a tiny dot.

items.t: If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of Giants.
items.d: He learned so much because people before him had already worked so hard. We build on each other.

items.t: I have no special talents. I am only passionately curious.
items.d: Wanting to know how things work can take you a very long way.

items.t: Imagination is more important than knowledge.
items.d: Facts are useful, but new ideas start when you imagine what could be.

items.t: The important thing is not to stop questioning. Curiosity has its own reason for existing.
items.d: Keep asking why. Being curious is good all by itself.

items.t: Life is like riding a bicycle. To keep your balance you must keep moving.
items.d: He wrote this to his son. Keep trying and keep going, and you stay steady.

items.t: The most beautiful thing we can experience is the mysterious.
items.d: Things we do not understand yet are exciting, because they are waiting to be discovered.

items.t: It is possible to fly without motors, but not without knowledge and skill.
items.d: Before building a plane with an engine, the Wright brothers learned to fly gliders very carefully.

items.t: Nothing is too wonderful to be true, if it be consistent with the laws of nature.
items.d: Amazing things can be real, as long as they follow the rules of how nature works.

items.t: Work, finish, publish.
items.d: His advice to a young scientist: do the work, finish it, then share it with the world.

items.t: We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.
items.d: We may not know the whole future, but there is lots of useful work we can start right now.

items.t: The world needs all kinds of minds.
items.d: People think in different ways, and every way of thinking can help the world.

items.t: Remember to look up at the stars and not down at your feet.
items.d: Stay curious about the big world around you, and keep wondering.

items.t: This is for everyone.
items.d: The inventor of the World Wide Web wanted it to be free for all people to use.

items.t: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
items.d: The first step on the Moon in 1969 was tiny for one person but huge for all people.

items.t: We choose to go to the Moon in this decade... not because they are easy, but because they are hard.
items.d: Doing hard things helps us grow and learn what we can really do.

items.t: The vast loneliness is awe-inspiring and it makes you realize just what you have back there on Earth.
items.d: Seeing Earth from the Moon showed him how special our home planet is.

items.t: Because it's there.
items.d: His answer when asked why he wanted to climb Mount Everest. Explorers love a big challenge.

items.t: The mountains are calling and I must go.
items.d: He loved nature so much that the wild places always pulled him outside to explore.

items.t: It is not half so important to know as to feel.
items.d: For children, loving and wondering about nature matters even more than learning its names.

items.t: The more that you read, the more things you will know. The more that you learn, the more places you'll go.
items.d: Reading opens doors to new ideas, new places and new adventures.

items.t: Today you are You, that is truer than true. There is no one alive who is Youer than You.
items.d: Nobody else is exactly like you, and that is something to celebrate.

items.t: You have brains in your head. You have feet in your shoes. You can steer yourself any direction you choose.
items.d: You can think for yourself and choose your own path.

items.t: Unless someone like you cares a whole awful lot, nothing is going to get better. It's not.
items.d: From The Lorax. If you care about something, like trees or animals, you can help it.

items.t: A person's a person, no matter how small.
items.d: Everyone matters, big or little, young or old.

items.t: Oh, the thinks you can think up if only you try!
items.d: Your imagination is full of ideas waiting for you to discover them.

items.t: I meant what I said and I said what I meant.
items.d: Horton the elephant keeps his promise. Being trustworthy means doing what you said you would.

items.t: You're off to Great Places! Today is your day! Your mountain is waiting, so... get on your way!
items.d: Big adventures start with a first step today.

items.t: If you have good thoughts they will shine out of your face like sunbeams and you will always look lovely.
items.d: Kind and happy thoughts show on your face and make you shine.

items.t: Those who don't believe in magic will never find it.
items.d: Stay open to wonder, and you will notice amazing things everywhere.

items.t: It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye.
items.d: From The Little Prince. The most important things, like love and friendship, you feel rather than see.

items.t: I am not afraid of storms, for I am learning how to sail my ship.
items.d: From Little Women. Hard times feel less scary when you are learning how to handle them.

items.t: Isn't it nice to think that tomorrow is a new day with no mistakes in it yet?
items.d: From Anne of Green Gables. Every morning is a fresh start.

items.t: All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us.
items.d: Gandalf says this in The Lord of the Rings. We cannot choose everything, but we choose what we do.

items.t: Not all those who wander are lost.
items.d: People who wander and explore may still know exactly where they are headed.

items.t: Why, sometimes I've believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast.
items.d: The White Queen in Through the Looking-Glass. Imagining impossible things is great practice for your mind.

items.t: Begin at the beginning, and go on till you come to the end: then stop.
items.d: From Alice in Wonderland. A simple plan for telling a story, or doing almost any job.

items.t: It's no use going back to yesterday, because I was a different person then.
items.d: Alice says this. We grow and change every day.

items.t: You have been my friend. That in itself is a tremendous thing.
items.d: Charlotte the spider says this in Charlotte's Web. Friendship is a gift in itself.

items.t: There is nothing, absolutely nothing, half so much worth doing as simply messing about in boats.
items.d: Ratty says this in The Wind in the Willows. Simple fun outdoors is one of life's best things.

items.t: The world is so full of a number of things, I'm sure we should all be as happy as kings.
items.d: There are so many wonderful things to see and do. That is a good reason to be happy.

items.t: Just living is not enough... one must have sunshine, freedom, and a little flower.
items.d: A butterfly says this in his story. Small joys like sunshine and flowers make life sweet.

items.t: Two roads diverged in a wood, and I, I took the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference.
items.d: In his poem, a traveler chooses one path and later feels that this choice mattered.

items.t: Anything can happen, child. Anything can be.
items.d: From a poem in Where the Sidewalk Ends. The future is full of possibilities.

items.t: Their names are What and Why and When and How and Where and Who.
items.d: Kipling said these six question words were his helpers that taught him all he knew.

items.t: Always do right. This will gratify some people and astonish the rest.
items.d: Doing the right thing makes people happy, and surprises the ones who did not expect it.

items.t: How wonderful it is that nobody need wait a single moment before starting to improve the world.
items.d: You do not have to be grown up to help. You can start making things better right now.

items.t: Optimism is the faith that leads to achievement. Nothing can be done without hope and confidence.
items.d: Believing things can go well helps you work hard and reach your goals.

items.t: Life is either a daring adventure, or nothing.
items.d: She could not see or hear, yet she lived boldly. Try new things and be brave.

items.t: Although the world is full of suffering, it is full also of the overcoming of it.
items.d: People face hard things, but people are also very good at getting through them.

items.t: Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that. Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.
items.d: Being mean back does not fix meanness. Kindness is what makes things better.

items.t: I learned that courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it.
items.d: Brave people still feel scared, but they do not let fear stop them.

items.t: One child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world.
items.d: She spoke at the United Nations about why every child should get to go to school.

items.t: You must do the thing you think you cannot do.
items.d: Trying something that feels too hard is how you find out you are stronger than you thought.

items.t: Never give in, never give in, never, never, never, never.
items.d: He said this to students at his old school. Keep trying, even when things are tough.

items.t: Always bear in mind that your own resolution to succeed is more important than any other one thing.
items.d: From a letter to a young man. Your own decision to keep trying matters most.

items.t: Far and away the best prize that life has to offer is the chance to work hard at work worth doing.
items.d: Working hard on something that really matters is one of the best feelings there is.

items.t: I cannot live without books.
items.d: He loved reading so much he wrote this in a letter to his friend John Adams.

items.t: Well done is better than well said.
items.d: Doing something is better than just talking about it.

items.t: Lost time is never found again.
items.d: Use your time well, because you cannot get it back.

items.t: Pressure is a privilege.
items.d: Feeling nervous before a big moment means you have earned a chance to do something special.

items.t: You can observe a lot by watching.
items.d: A funny way of saying: pay attention and you will learn a lot.

items.t: It ain't over till it's over.
items.d: Do not give up early. Things can still change before the end.

items.t: We don't make mistakes, just happy little accidents.
items.d: A painter's way of saying a mistake can turn into something new and nice.

items.t: There's no person in the whole world like you, and I like you just the way you are.
items.d: Mister Rogers told children on TV that each of them was special.

items.t: Gravity pulls things toward Earth.
items.d: When you drop a sock, gravity pulls it to the floor.

items.t: Friction can slow things that slide.
items.d: A book pushed across a table slows down as it rubs against the table.

items.t: Moving things tend to keep moving.
items.d: When the car stops, your seat belt stops you from moving forward.

items.t: The same push speeds up a light cart more than a heavy cart.
items.d: With an equal push, an empty shopping cart speeds up faster than a full one.

items.t: A push is met by an equal push in the other direction.
items.d: Push water backward with your hands as you swim. The water pushes you forward.

items.t: Light bounces off a mirror.
items.d: When you brush your teeth, light from your face bounces off the mirror into your eyes.

items.t: Light can bend when it goes from water into air.
items.d: A straw in a clear glass of water can look bent at the water line.

items.t: Sounds start with something shaking back and forth.
items.d: Pluck a guitar string and watch it shake as it makes a sound.

items.t: Faster shaking makes a higher note.
items.d: On a guitar, pressing a string closer to the bridge leaves less string to shake and makes a higher note.

items.t: Heat moves from warmer things to cooler things.
items.d: A metal spoon warms up when you leave it in hot soup.

items.t: Water pushes upward on things in it.
items.d: A beach ball pops up when you let it go underwater.

items.t: A push farther from a pivot can turn something more easily.
items.d: A door swings open more easily when you push near the handle than when you push near the hinges.

items.t: Two north poles of magnets push each other away.
items.d: Bring the north ends of two toy bar magnets together and feel them push apart.

items.t: Electric current needs a complete path to keep flowing in a simple circuit.
items.d: A flashlight switch breaks the path when you turn it off.

items.t: Rubbing materials together can build up an electric charge.
items.d: Rub a balloon on your hair. The balloon can then pull your hair toward it.

items.t: A feather and a hammer fall together when there is no air.
items.d: Astronauts showed this on the Moon. On Earth, air slows the feather.

items.t: Air pushes against things moving through it. This is air resistance.
items.d: You feel it push on your face when you ride a bike fast.

items.t: A parachute has a big surface, so air slows its fall a lot.
items.d: The wide cloth catches lots of air, so the jumper drifts down gently.

items.t: Flat paper falls slower than the same paper crumpled into a ball.
items.d: The flat sheet catches more air, so air pushes up on it more.

items.t: A streamlined shape slides through air more easily.
items.d: Cyclists crouch low and wear smooth helmets to cut through the wind.

items.t: Weight is the pull of gravity on an object.
items.d: You weigh less on the Moon because the Moon pulls more gently.

items.t: Mass is how much stuff is in something. It stays the same everywhere.
items.d: A bag of flour holds the same amount of flour on Earth or the Moon.

items.t: Rough surfaces make more friction than smooth ones.
items.d: Sandpaper grips your hand more than a smooth sheet of plastic.

items.t: Friction turns movement into heat.
items.d: Rub your hands together fast and they get warm.

items.t: Wet ice has very little friction, so things slide easily.
items.d: Ice skates glide, but your shoes slip on a wet icy path.

items.t: A force is a push or a pull.
items.d: You push a swing. You pull a wagon.

items.t: Unbalanced forces change how something moves.
items.d: A bigger pull from one team drags the rope and the other team.

items.t: A rocket moves up by pushing hot gas down.
items.d: A balloon zooms the other way when you let its air rush out.

items.t: When you jump off a skateboard, the board rolls backward.
items.d: Your push on the board is matched by its push on you.

items.t: A pendulum swings back and forth with a steady beat.
items.d: A playground swing takes about the same time for each swing.

items.t: A longer pendulum swings more slowly.
items.d: A swing on long chains takes longer per swing than one on short chains.

items.t: Something moving in a circle keeps changing direction.
items.d: A car going around a roundabout is always turning, even at steady speed.

items.t: Speed tells how far something goes in a set time.
items.d: A bike going 10 km in one hour has a speed of 10 km per hour.

items.t: A ball thrown sideways still falls at the same time as one dropped.
items.d: Both hit the ground together, but the thrown one lands farther away.

items.t: A ball thrown in an arc follows a curved path.
items.d: A basketball shot rises, slows, then curves down into the hoop.

items.t: Pressure is a push spread over an area.
items.d: The same push on a small spot presses harder than on a big spot.

items.t: A sharp knife cuts better because its edge is very thin.
items.d: All your push goes onto a tiny edge, so the pressure is high.

items.t: Water pressure gets bigger the deeper you go.
items.d: Your ears can feel it when you dive to the bottom of a pool.

items.t: Air has weight, and it pushes on everything around us.
items.d: A sealed bag of chips looks puffy up a mountain because outside air pushes less.

items.t: A drinking straw works because air pushes on the drink.
items.d: You make low pressure in the straw and the air pushes juice up.

items.t: A heavy ship floats because it is shaped to hold lots of air.
items.d: Its wide hollow shape pushes aside enough water to hold it up.

items.t: Something floats if it is less dense than the liquid.
items.d: A cork floats in water because it is lighter for its size.

items.t: Light travels in straight lines.
items.d: Sunbeams through a gap in the curtains look like straight streaks.

items.t: A shadow forms when something blocks light.
items.d: Stand in sunshine and your body blocks the light behind you.

items.t: Light moves much faster than sound.
items.d: You see lightning first and hear the thunder a little later.

items.t: Clear things let light through. Opaque things block light.
items.d: You can see through a window, but not through a wooden door.

items.t: A white light can split into a rainbow of colors.
items.d: A glass prism or raindrops can bend each color a different amount.

items.t: A rainbow forms when sunlight passes through raindrops.
items.d: The drops bend the light and spread it into colors.

items.t: A red apple looks red because it bounces red light to your eyes.
items.d: It soaks up most other colors of light that hit it.

items.t: Dark clothes get warmer in the sun than light clothes.
items.d: A black T-shirt feels hotter than a white one on a sunny day.

items.t: A smooth mirror shows a clear picture, but rough surfaces do not.
items.d: Still water works like a mirror, but a rippled pond does not.

items.t: A magnifying glass is a curved piece of glass that bends light.
items.d: It makes small things like ants look bigger.

items.t: Your eyes see because light bounces off things and enters them.
items.d: In a completely dark room, you cannot see anything at all.

items.t: Sound travels as waves of vibration through air.
items.d: Shout across a field and the air carries the shaking to a friend.

items.t: Sound cannot travel through empty space.
items.d: With no air to shake, space is silent.

items.t: Sound travels faster through water than through air.
items.d: Underwater, you can hear a splash from a long way off.

items.t: Sound travels through solid things too.
items.d: Put your ear on a table and tap the far end. It sounds louder.

items.t: An echo is sound that bounces off a hard surface.
items.d: Shout in a tunnel or an empty hall and your voice comes back.

items.t: A bigger vibration makes a louder sound.
items.d: Hit a drum hard and the skin shakes more, so it is louder.

items.t: Metal is a good conductor of heat. Heat moves through it quickly.
items.d: A metal spoon in hot soup soon feels hot at the handle.

items.t: Wood and plastic are poor conductors of heat.
items.d: Pot handles are plastic or wood so they stay cooler to hold.

items.t: Insulation slows down heat moving from place to place.
items.d: A woolly hat keeps your body heat from escaping.

items.t: Trapped air is a great insulator.
items.d: A puffy coat is warm because tiny pockets of air hold your heat in.

items.t: A vacuum flask keeps drinks hot or cold by slowing heat transfer.
items.d: Its double walls have almost no air between them to carry heat.

items.t: Metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature.
items.d: It pulls heat from your hand faster, so your skin feels cold.

items.t: Warm air rises, and cool air sinks.
items.d: The air near the ceiling of a room is warmer than near the floor.

items.t: Heat can travel as rays you feel, without touching.
items.d: You feel warmth from a campfire or the Sun on your face.

items.t: Most things get bigger when heated and smaller when cooled.
items.d: Bridges have small gaps so they can stretch safely in hot weather.

items.t: A liquid thermometer works because the liquid in it expands when it warms.
items.d: The liquid rises up the thin tube as the temperature goes up.

items.t: Heat is energy moving, and temperature tells how hot something is.
items.d: A bathtub of warm water stores more energy than a cup at the same temperature.

items.t: Water takes a long time to heat up and cool down.
items.d: The sea stays cool on a hot day, and the sand gets very hot.

items.t: Moving things have movement energy, called kinetic energy.
items.d: A fast rolling ball can knock over more skittles than a slow one.

items.t: Things held up high have stored energy from gravity.
items.d: A child at the top of a slide has stored energy that turns into motion.

items.t: A stretched rubber band stores energy.
items.d: Let go of it and it zips across the room.

items.t: Food gives your body stored energy to move and grow.
items.d: A good breakfast gives you energy to run around at break time.

items.t: Plants store energy from sunlight in their leaves and food.
items.d: Sunlight helps plants grow, and animals get energy by eating them.

items.t: A battery stores energy ready to turn into light, sound or motion.
items.d: A torch turns battery energy into light.

items.t: A bouncing ball loses a little energy each bounce.
items.d: Some turns into sound and heat, so it bounces lower each time.

items.t: Solar panels turn light from the Sun into electricity.
items.d: Some calculators run on a small solar panel with no battery.

items.t: A wind turbine turns the movement of wind into electricity.
items.d: The wind spins the blades and a generator makes power.

items.t: A bulb in a circuit lights up when current passes through it.
items.d: A torch lights only when the switch completes the path.

items.t: Metals like copper let electricity flow easily. They are conductors.
items.d: Wires are made of copper, with a plastic cover around them.

items.t: Rubber and plastic do not let electricity flow. They are insulators.
items.d: The plastic coating on a charger cable keeps the electricity inside.

items.t: A magnet pulls on iron and steel, but not on wood or plastic.
items.d: A fridge magnet clings to the steel door, but not to a wooden shelf.

items.t: The Earth acts like a giant magnet.
items.d: A compass needle lines up with Earth's magnetic field and points north.

items.t: A magnet has two ends called poles, a north and a south.
items.d: If you cut a magnet in half, each piece has both poles.

items.t: A magnet's push or pull works through paper and thin plastic.
items.d: A magnet can move a paper clip across a table from underneath.

items.t: Opposite electric charges attract. Matching charges push apart.
items.d: Hair stands up after a balloon rub because the strands push each other.

items.t: A lever turns around a fixed point, called a fulcrum.
items.d: A seesaw turns on its middle so one end goes up as the other goes down.

items.t: A longer lever lets you lift a heavy thing with a smaller push.
items.d: A long crowbar can pry up a heavy lid more easily than a short one.

items.t: A wheelbarrow is a lever that helps you carry heavy loads.
items.d: Lifting the handles takes less effort than lifting the load by hand.

items.t: A ramp lets you raise something with less force, over a longer path.
items.d: It is easier to push a box up a slope than to lift it straight up.

items.t: A screw is a ramp wrapped around a pole.
items.d: It turns and pulls itself into wood, going down a tiny slope.

items.t: A wedge is two ramps joined together.
items.d: An axe or a knife splits things apart by pushing sideways as it goes in.

items.t: A pulley uses a rope and wheel to change the direction of a pull.
items.d: A flag goes up when you pull the rope down.

items.t: Gears are wheels with teeth that turn each other.
items.d: On a bike, the gears help you pedal up steep hills.

items.t: Simple machines make a job easier, but they do not give free energy.
items.d: A ramp needs less push, but you must push over a longer distance.

items.t: Things are steadier with a low center of gravity.
items.d: A tall, narrow stack of books tips over more easily than a wide pile.

items.t: The center of gravity is the point where an object balances.
items.d: A ruler balances on your finger at its middle.

items.t: A wide base makes things hard to tip over.
items.d: A traffic cone sits steadily on its wide square bottom.

items.t: Bending your knees helps you stay balanced.
items.d: On a skateboard you crouch to keep your weight low and steady.

items.t: A longer stopping time means a smaller force.
items.d: Bending your knees when you land from a jump makes the landing softer.

items.t: An elastic thing springs back to its shape after being stretched.
items.d: A trampoline stretches down and then pushes you back up.

items.t: Lightning is a huge spark of static electricity.
items.d: It is like the spark you may see taking off a woolly jumper, but much bigger.

items.t: Tires have treads, grooves that help them grip the road.
items.d: Even on a wet road, the grooves help the tire hold on.

items.t: Wide snowshoes stop you sinking into snow.
items.d: Your weight spreads over a big area, so the pressure is smaller.

items.t: Oil floats on water because it is less dense.
items.d: Oil drops in soup gather on top instead of mixing in.

items.t: Salty water pushes up harder than fresh water.
items.d: It feels easier to float in the sea than in a swimming pool.

items.t: A hot air balloon rises because hot air is lighter than cool air.
items.d: The warm air inside is less dense than the cool air outside.

items.t: Fill glasses with different amounts of water to make different notes.
items.d: Tap a glass with more water and the note sounds lower.

items.t: Soft things soak up sound.
items.d: A room with thick curtains and rugs sounds quieter than an empty room.

items.t: A big drum makes a deeper sound than a small drum.
items.d: A bass drum goes boom, while a little drum goes tap.

items.t: A shadow is longest when the Sun is low in the sky.
items.d: Your shadow is very long in the late afternoon.

items.t: A wheel on an axle rolls with less friction than sliding.
items.d: A trolley with wheels is easier to push than a box dragged on the floor.

items.t: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that still acts like that element.
items.d: Everything from air to apples is made of atoms.

items.t: Most of an atom's mass is packed into its tiny nucleus.
items.d: The nucleus sits at the center of the atom.

items.t: Protons are positively charged particles inside an atom's nucleus.
items.d: The number of protons tells you which element the atom is.

items.t: Neutrons have no electric charge and sit in an atom's nucleus.
items.d: A neutron is about as heavy as a proton.

items.t: Electrons are negatively charged particles found around an atom's nucleus.
items.d: Electrons help atoms join and react with one another.

items.t: An element's atomic number equals the number of protons in each of its atoms.
items.d: Every carbon atom has 6 protons, so carbon's atomic number is 6.

items.t: Each element has a short chemical symbol.
items.d: O means oxygen, C means carbon and Fe means iron.

items.t: The periodic table lists elements in order of atomic number.
items.d: Each step across the table adds one proton.

items.t: Elements in the same periodic table column often behave in similar ways.
items.d: Lithium, sodium and potassium share a column, and all are soft, shiny metals.

items.t: A molecule forms when two or more atoms join with chemical bonds.
items.d: A water molecule contains three atoms joined together.

items.t: A compound contains two or more different elements chemically joined.
items.d: Water is a compound made from hydrogen and oxygen.

items.t: The oxygen gas in air is mostly made of molecules with two oxygen atoms.
items.d: Its chemical formula is O2.

items.t: Each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
items.d: That is why water's formula is H2O.

items.t: Each carbon dioxide molecule has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
items.d: Its formula is CO2, and you breathe some out.

items.t: Table salt contains sodium ions and chloride ions in a 1 to 1 ratio.
items.d: Its chemical formula is NaCl.

items.t: An ion is an atom or group of atoms with an electric charge.
items.d: It becomes charged by losing or gaining electrons.

items.t: An atom that loses electrons becomes a positive ion.
items.d: A sodium atom can lose one electron to become a sodium ion.

items.t: An atom that gains electrons becomes a negative ion.
items.d: A chlorine atom can gain one electron to become a chloride ion.

items.t: A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons.
items.d: Hydrogen and oxygen share electrons in a water molecule.

items.t: An ionic bond is the attraction between positive and negative ions.
items.d: This attraction holds sodium and chloride ions together in salt.

items.t: Isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.d: All carbon isotopes have 6 protons, but their neutron counts can differ.

items.t: A solid keeps its own shape and volume.
items.d: Its particles stay close together and vibrate in place.

items.t: A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
items.d: Juice changes shape when poured from a carton into a glass.

items.t: A gas has no fixed shape or volume.
items.d: Air spreads out to fill a balloon.

items.t: Melting changes a solid into a liquid.
items.d: An ice cube melts into liquid water as it warms.

items.t: Freezing changes a liquid into a solid.
items.d: Liquid water becomes ice in a freezer.

items.t: Evaporation happens when particles escape from a liquid's surface.
items.d: A wet pavement slowly dries even when the water is not boiling.

items.t: Boiling happens throughout a liquid, not only at its surface.
items.d: Bubbles of water vapor form throughout boiling water.

items.t: Condensation changes a gas into a liquid.
items.d: Water vapor can form drops on the outside of a cold glass.

items.t: Sublimation changes a solid directly into a gas.
items.d: Snow can slowly disappear on a cold, dry day without first melting.

items.t: Deposition changes a gas directly into a solid.
items.d: Water vapor can form ice crystals as frost on a cold surface.

items.t: Plasma is a gas-like state containing charged particles.
items.d: Stars are mostly plasma.

items.t: Heating matter usually makes its particles move faster.
items.d: Warm food gives off smells faster because particles move and spread more quickly.

items.t: A gas can be squeezed into a smaller space more easily than a liquid.
items.d: Pushing a blocked bicycle pump compresses the trapped air.

items.t: Density tells how much mass is packed into a certain volume.
items.d: A stone is usually denser than an equal-sized piece of foam.

items.t: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
items.d: Ice cubes stay near the top of a drink.

items.t: Water expands when it freezes.
items.d: The same amount of water takes up more space as ice.

items.t: A pure substance has a fixed composition and its own set of properties.
items.d: Pure water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio.

items.t: A mixture contains substances together without chemically joining them.
items.d: A bowl of cereal and fruit is a mixture whose parts remain easy to see.

items.t: A solution is a mixture that looks the same throughout.
items.d: Salt can spread evenly through water to make a clear solution.

items.t: A solute dissolves in a solvent.
items.d: In sugar water, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent.

items.t: Concentration tells how much solute is in a certain amount of solution.
items.d: More drink powder in the same amount of water makes a stronger solution.

items.t: A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute at that temperature.
items.d: Extra sugar stays at the bottom once the water has dissolved all it can.

items.t: Stirring can make a solid dissolve faster.
items.d: Sugar dissolves faster when stirred because fresh water keeps reaching it.

items.t: Hot water can dissolve more sugar than the same amount of cold water.
items.d: Temperature can change how much of a substance will dissolve.

items.t: Crystals can form when particles in a solution arrange into a pattern.
items.d: Salt crystals may appear as salty water slowly evaporates.

items.t: Oil and water do not mix evenly.
items.d: After shaking, oil droplets usually join and rise into a separate layer.

items.t: A suspension has particles that may settle when left still.
items.d: Muddy water clears slowly as some soil sinks to the bottom.

items.t: A colloid has tiny particles spread through another substance.
items.d: Milk contains tiny fat droplets and proteins spread through water.

items.t: Filtering can separate an insoluble solid from a liquid.
items.d: A coffee filter traps solid grounds while the liquid passes through.

items.t: Evaporation can separate a dissolved solid from water.
items.d: When salt water evaporates, the salt remains behind.

items.t: Distillation separates substances by boiling and then condensing vapor.
items.d: Water vapor can be cooled and collected apart from dissolved salt.

items.t: Paper chromatography can separate some mixtures of colored dyes.
items.d: Some marker inks spread into several colors as water moves up paper.

items.t: A magnet can help separate iron from a mixture.
items.d: A magnet can lift iron filings away from sand.

items.t: An alloy is a mixture containing a metal and one or more other elements.
items.d: Alloys can have different properties from the elements used to make them.

items.t: Brass is an alloy made mainly from copper and zinc.
items.d: It often has a golden color and is used for musical instruments.

items.t: Steel is made mostly from iron with carbon and sometimes other elements.
items.d: Changing the mixture can make different kinds of steel.

items.t: Air is a mixture of gases, not a single substance.
items.d: Dry air is about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen.

items.t: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms into new substances.
items.d: The atoms remain, but their bonds and partners can change.

items.t: Mass is conserved during a chemical reaction in a closed container.
items.d: The total mass before and after the reaction stays the same.

items.t: Bubbles, a color change or a new solid can be clues that a reaction occurred.
items.d: One clue alone does not always prove that a new substance formed.

items.t: A temperature change can be a clue to a chemical reaction.
items.d: Some reactions warm their surroundings, while others cool them.

items.t: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up overall.
items.d: Enzymes act as catalysts for many reactions in your body.

items.t: Many reactions need some starting energy called activation energy.
items.d: A spark supplies starting energy when a gas stove is safely switched on.

items.t: An exothermic reaction releases energy to its surroundings.
items.d: Disposable hand warmers get warm as iron powder inside slowly rusts.

items.t: An endothermic reaction takes in energy from its surroundings.
items.d: Photosynthesis stores energy from sunlight in sugar.

items.t: Burning is a chemical reaction that usually involves oxygen.
items.d: A candle flame releases heat and light as wax vapor reacts with oxygen.

items.t: Photosynthesis changes carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
items.d: Plants use light energy to power this chemical process.

items.t: Many cells use oxygen to release energy from food.
items.d: This process produces carbon dioxide and water.

items.t: Iron rusts when it reacts with oxygen in the presence of water.
items.d: Keeping an iron tool clean and dry helps slow rusting.

items.t: Salty water can make iron rust faster.
items.d: Dissolved ions help electric charges move during the rusting process.

items.t: Silver can tarnish by reacting with sulfur compounds in the air.
items.d: The reaction forms a dark coating on the silver's surface.

items.t: Copper can slowly form a green patina after reacting with air and water.
items.d: The coating is made of new copper compounds.

items.t: The pH scale tells how acidic or basic a water-based solution is.
items.d: A pH meter or indicator paper can measure it.

items.t: Acidic solutions have a pH below 7 on the common pH scale.
items.d: Lemon juice is acidic because it contains citric acid.

items.t: Basic solutions have a pH above 7 on the common pH scale.
items.d: A solution of baking soda and water is mildly basic.

items.t: Pure water is neutral, with a pH of 7 at about 25 degrees Celsius.
items.d: Neutral means it is neither acidic nor basic.

items.t: A chemical indicator changes color depending on acidity.
items.d: Indicator paper can show whether a solution is acidic or basic.

items.t: Red cabbage contains pigments that can act as a pH indicator.
items.d: The pigments show different colors in acidic and basic liquids.

items.t: An acid and a base can react to form a salt and water.
items.d: This kind of reaction is called neutralization.

items.t: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when it reacts with an acid.
items.d: The gas forms the bubbles when baking soda meets lemon juice.

items.t: Yeast can turn sugars into carbon dioxide and other substances.
items.d: The gas makes bubbles that help bread dough puff up.

items.t: Baking powder contains ingredients that can produce carbon dioxide gas.
items.d: The bubbles help cakes and muffins rise while baking.

items.t: Heat changes the shape and links of proteins in an egg.
items.d: This chemical change turns a runny egg white firm.

items.t: Starch grains swell and thicken mixtures when heated with water.
items.d: Starch can make soup or sauce less runny.

items.t: Browning toast creates new flavors through reactions between sugars and proteins.
items.d: These are called Maillard reactions.

items.t: Caramelization happens when sugar molecules change as they are heated.
items.d: The change creates brown colors and new flavors.

items.t: A soap molecule has a water-loving end and an oil-loving end.
items.d: This lets soap connect oily dirt with water.

items.t: Soap can surround grease in tiny droplets that water carries away.
items.d: That is why washing works better with soap than with water alone.

items.t: Detergents lower water's surface tension.
items.d: This helps water spread through fabric and reach dirt.

items.t: Hard water contains noticeable amounts of dissolved calcium and magnesium ions.
items.d: These minerals can leave a pale scale inside a kettle.

items.t: A polymer is a large molecule built from many smaller repeating units.
items.d: Many plastics are polymers with long chains of repeating parts.

items.t: Cellulose is a natural polymer found in plant cell walls.
items.d: Paper and cotton contain lots of cellulose.

items.t: Rubber contains long polymer chains that can uncoil when stretched.
items.d: The chains help a rubber band return toward its original shape.

items.t: Glass is a solid, not a liquid that slowly flows.
items.d: Its particles are locked in place but lack the neat pattern of a crystal.

items.t: Diamond and graphite are different forms of the element carbon.
items.d: Their carbon atoms are arranged differently, giving them different properties.

items.t: Noble gases react very little with other elements.
items.d: Helium, a noble gas, is used to fill some balloons.

items.t: Pure water conducts electricity poorly, but dissolved ions improve conduction.
items.d: Salt water conducts better because its moving ions carry electric charge.

items.t: To triple a number, add three copies of it.
items.d: Triple 7 is 7 + 7 + 7 = 21.

items.t: Adding two odd numbers gives an even number.
items.d: 5 + 7 = 12. You can split 12 into two equal groups of 6.

items.t: Swap the numbers you multiply and the answer stays the same.
items.d: 3 rows of 4 dots make 12 dots. Turn the page sideways and you get 4 rows of 3, still 12.

items.t: To multiply by 9, multiply by 10 and take away one copy.
To multiply a whole number by 5, multiply by 10 and halve the result.
items.d: For 5 × 14, first find 10 × 14 = 140. Half of 140 is 70.

items.t: A whole number is divisible by 3 if its digits add up to a multiple of 3.
items.d: For 42, add 4 + 2 = 6. Since 6 is a multiple of 3, 42 divides by 3 exactly. 42 ÷ 3 = 14.

items.t: Fractions stay equal when you multiply the top and bottom by the same nonzero number.
items.d: Multiply the 1 and 2 in 1/2 by 3. You get 3/6, which is still half.

items.t: To find a quarter of something, divide it into four equal parts.
items.d: A quarter of 20 grapes is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 grapes.

items.t: A rectangle's area is its length times its width.
items.d: A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle has area 6 × 4 = 24 square centimeters.

items.t: For a shape with straight sides, add the side lengths to find the distance around it.
items.d: A rectangle with sides 8 cm and 3 cm is 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22 cm around.

items.t: The three angles of a triangle on flat paper always add up to 180°.
items.d: With angles of 90° and 35°, the last angle is 180° - 90° - 35° = 55°.

items.t: A circle's diameter is twice its radius.
items.d: If it's 4 cm from the center to the edge, it's 2 × 4 = 8 cm all the way across the center.

items.t: A prime number has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.
items.d: Only 1 and 7 divide 7 with no leftover, so 7 is prime.

items.t: An average is the amount everyone would get if the total were shared equally.
items.d: Three friends have 2, 4 and 9 stickers. That's 15 stickers, so the average is 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

items.t: To find 10 percent of a number, divide it by 10.
items.d: 10 percent of 80 is 80 ÷ 10 = 8.

items.t: To double a number, add it to itself.
items.d: Double 18 is 18 + 18 = 36.

items.t: To halve an even whole number, split it into two equal groups.
items.d: Half of 46 is 46 ÷ 2 = 23.

items.t: To add 9, add 10 and then subtract 1.
To add 99, add 100 and then subtract 1.
To subtract 9, subtract 10 and then add 1.
To multiply by 4, double the number twice.
To multiply by 8, double the number three times.
items.d: 7 becomes 14, then 28, then 56. So 8 × 7 = 56.

items.t: For the numbers 1 to 9, multiplying by 11 repeats the digit.
To multiply by 25, divide by 4 and multiply by 100.
To multiply by 50, multiply by 100 and then halve.
To divide by 5, double the number and divide by 10.
Dividing by 10 makes each digit worth one tenth as much.
Multiplying by 10 makes each digit worth 10 times as much.
Any number multiplied by zero equals zero.
Multiplying a number by 1 leaves it unchanged.
You can split a multiplication into easier parts.
You can regroup numbers when adding without changing the sum.
Addition and subtraction can undo each other.
Multiplication and division facts can form a fact family.
Rounding can give a quick estimate before exact calculation.
items.d: 198 + 304 is about 200 + 300 = 500. The exact sum is 502.

items.t: A digit's place tells how much that digit is worth.
items.d: In 4,582, the 5 is worth 500.

items.t: Expanded form shows the value of every digit.
Compare whole numbers from their greatest place value first.
items.d: 5,284 > 5,249 because 8 tens is greater than 4 tens.

items.t: To round to the nearest ten, look at the ones digit.
items.d: 347 rounds to 350 because its ones digit is 7.

items.t: To round to the nearest hundred, look at the tens digit.
items.d: 3,649 rounds to 3,600 because its tens digit is 4.

items.t: Negative numbers are less than zero.
items.d: On a number line, -3 is three steps left of 0.

items.t: Opposite numbers add to zero.
Absolute value is a number's distance from zero.
items.d: Both 7 and -7 are 7 steps from zero, so both have absolute value 7.

items.t: Parentheses tell you which calculation to do first.
An equation says that two amounts are equal.
items.d: 7 + 5 = 3 × 4 because both sides equal 12.

items.t: A whole number is divisible by 2 when its last digit is even.
items.d: 1,438 is divisible by 2 because its last digit is 8. 1,438 ÷ 2 = 719.

items.t: A whole number is divisible by 5 when it ends in 0 or 5.
A whole number is divisible by 10 when it ends in 0.
A number is divisible by 9 if its digits add to a multiple of 9.
items.d: For 729, 7 + 2 + 9 = 18. Since 18 is a multiple of 9, 729 ÷ 9 = 81.

items.t: A number is divisible by 6 if it is divisible by both 2 and 3.
items.d: 54 is even. Its digits add to 5 + 4 = 9, so 54 is divisible by 3. So 54 ÷ 6 = 9.

items.t: A factor divides a whole number with no remainder.
items.d: 4 is a factor of 28 because 28 ÷ 4 = 7.

items.t: A multiple comes from multiplying a number by a whole number.
items.d: 35 is a multiple of 7 because 7 × 5 = 35.

items.t: The greatest common factor is the largest factor shared by two numbers.
items.d: The greatest common factor of 18 and 24 is 6.

items.t: The least common multiple is the smallest positive multiple two numbers share.
items.d: Multiples of 6 and 8 first meet at 24, so their least common multiple is 24.

items.t: A composite number has more than two positive factors.
items.d: 12 is composite because its factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.

items.t: The number 1 is neither prime nor composite.
items.d: It has only one positive factor, which is 1.

items.t: A square number is a whole number multiplied by itself.
items.d: 9 × 9 = 81, so 81 is a square number.

items.t: A cube number uses the same factor three times.
items.d: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27, so 27 is a cube number.

items.t: Odd numbers can be made by starting at 1 and adding 2 each time.
items.d: 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 are the first five positive odd numbers.

items.t: Triangular numbers come from adding consecutive counting numbers.
items.d: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, so 10 is a triangular number.

items.t: In the Fibonacci pattern, each new number is the sum of the previous two.
items.d: Starting 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, the next number is 3 + 5 = 8.

items.t: An even number times any whole number is even.
items.d: 14 × 7 = 98, which is even.

items.t: An odd number times an odd number is odd.
items.d: 7 × 9 = 63, which is odd.

items.t: Consecutive whole numbers differ by 1.
items.d: 46 and 47 are consecutive because 47 - 46 = 1.

items.t: To add 1 + 2 + ... up to n, work out n × (n + 1) ÷ 2.
The top number of a fraction, the numerator, tells how many equal parts we count.
items.d: In 3/8, the whole has 8 equal parts, and the numerator 3 means three of them are counted.

items.t: A proper fraction has a numerator smaller than its denominator.
items.d: 5/7 is proper because 5 < 7.

items.t: An improper fraction can be written as a mixed number.
items.d: 11/4 = 2 3/4 because 11 ÷ 4 gives 2 with 3 left over.

items.t: With equal denominators, the larger numerator makes the larger fraction.
For positive fractions with equal numerators, the smaller denominator makes the larger fraction.
items.d: 3/5 > 3/8 because fifths are larger than eighths.

items.t: Add fractions with equal denominators by adding their numerators.
Subtract fractions with equal denominators by subtracting their numerators.
To find a fraction of a number, divide by the bottom and multiply by the top.
items.d: To find 3/5 of 40, calculate 40 ÷ 5 × 3 = 24.

items.t: A nonzero fraction times its reciprocal equals 1.
The first digit after a decimal point shows tenths.
items.d: In 3.7, the 7 means 7/10.

items.t: The second digit after a decimal point shows hundredths.
items.d: In 2.46, the 6 means 6/100.

items.t: One half equals 0.5.
One fourth equals 0.25.
Line up decimal points when adding decimals.
Fifty percent means one half.
items.d: 50 percent of 36 is 36 ÷ 2 = 18.

items.t: Twenty percent means one fifth.
items.d: 20 percent of 45 is 45 ÷ 5 = 9.

items.t: Seventy-five percent means three fourths.
items.d: 75 percent of 20 is 20 ÷ 4 × 3 = 15.

items.t: Percent means parts out of 100.
A ratio compares amounts using the same order each time.
items.d: With 6 red beads and 3 blue beads, the red-to-blue ratio is 6:3, or 2:1.

items.t: Equivalent ratios come from multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number.
items.d: 3:5 and 12:20 are equal ratios because 3 × 4 = 12 and 5 × 4 = 20.

items.t: Opposite angles made by two crossing straight lines are equal.
items.d: If one angle is 48°, the angle directly opposite it is also 48°.

items.t: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and two equal angles.
items.d: If two angles are 70° each, the third is 180° - 70° - 70° = 40°.

items.t: A trapezoid's area is the average of its parallel sides times its height.
items.d: With parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm, its area is (6 + 10) ÷ 2 × 4 = 32 cm².

items.t: A triangle's area is half its base times its height.
items.d: A triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm has area 10 × 6 ÷ 2 = 30 cm².

items.t: A parallelogram's area is its base times its perpendicular height.
items.d: With base 9 cm and height 4 cm, its area is 9 × 4 = 36 cm².

items.t: A right angle measures exactly 90°.
items.d: A square has four 90° angles, and 4 × 90° = 360°.

items.t: A straight angle is 180°, and a full turn is 360°.
items.d: Two straight angles make one full turn because 180° + 180° = 360°.

items.t: The four angles of a quadrilateral on flat paper add up to 360°.
items.d: If three angles are 90°, the last is 360° - 270° = 90°.

items.t: Shape names can tell you how many sides they have.
items.d: A pentagon has 5 sides, a hexagon has 6, and an octagon has 8.

items.t: A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles.
items.d: Each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°, and 6 × 120° = 720°.

items.t: A line of symmetry splits a shape into matching mirror halves.
items.d: A square has 4 lines of symmetry.

items.t: Coordinates name a point using its horizontal position first.
items.d: From (2, 3) to (7, 3), the horizontal distance is 7 - 2 = 5 units.

items.t: Congruent shapes have the same shape and the same size.
items.d: Two 3 cm by 5 cm rectangles are congruent, and each has area 3 × 5 = 15 cm².

items.t: Similar shapes have the same shape, but they may have different sizes.
items.d: A 3 cm by 4 cm rectangle and a 6 cm by 8 cm rectangle are similar because both sides doubled.

items.t: In a right triangle, the two shorter sides help find the longest side.
items.d: For sides 3, 4 and 5, 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5².

items.t: A circle's circumference equals π times its diameter.
items.d: A circle with diameter 10 cm has circumference exactly 10π cm, about 31.4 cm.

items.t: A circle's area equals π times its radius squared.
items.d: A circle with radius 3 cm has area exactly 9π cm², about 28.3 cm².

items.t: One meter equals 100 centimeters.
items.d: 2.4 meters = 2.4 × 100 = 240 centimeters.

items.t: One kilometer equals 1,000 meters.
items.d: 3.5 kilometers = 3.5 × 1,000 = 3,500 meters.

items.t: One kilogram equals 1,000 grams.
One liter equals 1,000 milliliters.
items.d: 1.5 liters = 1.5 × 1,000 = 1,500 milliliters.

items.t: One hour equals 60 minutes.
items.d: 2 hours 15 minutes = 2 × 60 + 15 = 135 minutes.

items.t: Elapsed time is the difference between a start time and an end time.
items.d: From 2:35 to 4:05 is 1 hour 30 minutes.

items.t: A rectangular box's volume is length times width times height.
items.d: A 5 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm box has volume 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 cm³.

items.t: The median is the middle value after numbers are put in order.
items.d: For 2, 4, 7, 8 and 12, the median is 7.

items.t: For equally likely outcomes, probability is favorable outcomes divided by all outcomes.
items.d: A fair die has 3 even faces out of 6, so the chance of rolling an even number is 3/6 = 1/2.

items.t: A light-year is a distance, not a time.
items.d: It is how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers.

items.t: A parsec is a distance used by astronomers.
items.d: One parsec is about 3.26 light-years.

items.t: Looking far into space also means looking into the past.
items.d: We see a star 100 light-years away as it looked 100 years ago.

items.t: Stars twinkle because moving air bends their light.
items.d: Earth's atmosphere makes the light shift slightly from moment to moment.

items.t: Planets usually twinkle less than stars.
items.d: Their tiny disks of light are steadier when seen through moving air.

items.t: A star's color gives a clue to its surface temperature.
items.d: Blue stars are hotter than red stars.

items.t: A star can look bright because it is powerful, close, or both.
items.d: Distance changes how bright a star appears from Earth.

items.t: Nearly every star you can see without a telescope is in our Milky Way galaxy.
items.d: Other galaxies are much farther away and usually look like faint patches.

items.t: A constellation is a named area of the sky with a star pattern.
items.d: Its stars may be very different distances from Earth.

items.t: Astronomers divide the whole sky into 88 official constellations.
items.d: Together, they work like a map of the sky.

items.t: The Northern and Southern Hemispheres see different parts of the sky.
items.d: Some constellations never rise above the horizon in the other hemisphere.

items.t: Different constellations are easy to see in different seasons.
items.d: Earth faces different directions at night as it travels around the Sun.

items.t: From some places on Earth, a circumpolar constellation never sets below the horizon.
items.d: It seems to circle a sky pole during the night.

items.t: Polaris appears close to the north sky pole.
items.d: In the Northern Hemisphere, it can help observers find north.

items.t: Polaris is not the brightest star in the night sky.
items.d: Sirius appears brighter from Earth.

items.t: The Big Dipper is an asterism, not an official constellation.
items.d: Its seven bright stars are part of Ursa Major.

items.t: The ecliptic is the Sun's yearly path across our sky.
items.d: The Moon and planets also appear close to this path.

items.t: The zodiac constellations lie along the ecliptic.
items.d: The Sun appears to pass in front of them during the year.

items.t: Moon phases repeat about every 29.5 days.
items.d: This is the time from one new Moon to the next.

items.t: At new Moon, the Moon appears close to the Sun in our sky.
items.d: Its sunlit half faces mostly away from Earth.

items.t: At full Moon, Earth is roughly between the Sun and Moon.
items.d: The side facing Earth appears fully lit.

items.t: At a quarter Moon, half of the Moon's visible face looks lit.
items.d: The name describes how far the Moon is through its monthly cycle.

items.t: A waxing Moon shows more of its lit side each night.
items.d: It changes from new Moon toward full Moon.

items.t: A waning Moon shows less of its lit side each night.
items.d: It changes from full Moon toward new Moon.

items.t: People around the world see the same Moon phase at the same moment.
items.d: The phase may look tilted differently from different places.

items.t: Earthshine can faintly light the dark part of a crescent Moon.
items.d: Sunlight reflects from Earth to the Moon and back to us.

items.t: A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow.
items.d: Earth blocks some sunlight that would normally reach the Moon.

items.t: A lunar eclipse can happen only at full Moon.
items.d: That is when the Moon can pass behind Earth compared with the Sun.

items.t: Eclipses do not happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted.
items.d: The Moon usually passes above or below the needed line.

items.t: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day on average.
items.d: Its motion around Earth changes where it appears against the stars.

items.t: A full Moon rises near sunset and sets near sunrise.
items.d: It appears roughly opposite the Sun in the sky.

items.t: The Moon looks about half a degree wide in the sky.
items.d: Your little finger at arm's length can cover it easily.

items.t: The Moon illusion makes a low Moon look larger than a high Moon.
items.d: Its actual size in the sky changes very little during one night.

items.t: The bright side of the Moon always points toward the Sun.
items.d: Even when the Sun is below the horizon, this can reveal its direction.

items.t: The Sun's faint outer atmosphere is called the corona.
items.d: It becomes visible around the blocked Sun during a total solar eclipse.

items.t: Stars make energy by squeezing hydrogen together to make helium.
items.d: This process is called nuclear fusion.

items.t: A stable star balances two effects.
items.d: Gravity pulls inward while hot gas and radiation push outward.

items.t: Stars begin inside cold clouds of gas and dust.
items.d: Gravity can pull parts of a cloud together into dense clumps.

items.t: A protostar is a young, warming clump that may become a star.
items.d: It becomes a star when fusion begins in its center.

items.t: Stars spend most of their lives in the main sequence stage.
items.d: During this stage, they fuse hydrogen into helium.

items.t: A star's mass strongly affects how its life unfolds.
items.d: Mass changes its temperature, brightness and lifetime.

items.t: Massive stars use their fuel faster than smaller stars.
items.d: Although they have more fuel, they usually have shorter lives.

items.t: A red giant is a star whose outer layers have greatly expanded.
items.d: Its surface cools as the star grows larger.

items.t: A Sun-like star can leave behind a white dwarf.
items.d: A white dwarf is the hot, dense core left after outer gas drifts away.

items.t: A white dwarf can hold about a star's mass in an Earth-sized sphere.
items.d: Its matter is packed extremely tightly.

items.t: Some massive stars finish with a brilliant explosion called a supernova.
items.d: The blast can scatter newly made elements into space.

items.t: A neutron star is the crushed core left by some supernovas.
items.d: It packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere about the size of a city.

items.t: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star that sends out beams.
items.d: The beams can appear as regular pulses when they sweep past Earth.

items.t: A black hole has a boundary called an event horizon.
items.d: Past this boundary, not even light can escape.

items.t: Black holes do not pull in everything around them like vacuum cleaners.
items.d: Far away, their gravity acts like the gravity of any object with the same mass.

items.t: A binary star system contains two stars orbiting each other.
items.d: Many stars are members of pairs or larger groups.

items.t: In an eclipsing binary, one star regularly passes in front of the other.
items.d: The system's combined light dims in a repeating pattern.

items.t: A variable star changes in brightness over time.
items.d: It may swell, shrink, pulse, or be partly blocked by a companion.

items.t: An open cluster is a loose group of stars born from one cloud.
items.d: Open clusters are often found in a galaxy's disk.

items.t: A globular cluster is a crowded, round group of old stars.
items.d: Some contain hundreds of thousands of stars.

items.t: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space.
items.d: Some nebulae form stars, while others contain material shed by stars.

items.t: An emission nebula glows because nearby hot stars energize its gas.
items.d: The Orion Nebula is a well-known example.

items.t: A reflection nebula shines by scattering nearby starlight.
items.d: Its gas and dust do not make their own visible light.

items.t: A dark nebula blocks light from stars behind it.
items.d: It can look like a dark shape against a bright background.

items.t: Stars formed much of the carbon and oxygen found in the universe.
items.d: Stellar processes build elements from lighter particles.

items.t: A star's spectrum can reveal which elements are in its atmosphere.
items.d: Each element leaves a special pattern of lines in the light.

items.t: A brown dwarf is not massive enough for steady hydrogen fusion.
items.d: It is more massive than a planet but less massive than a true star.

items.t: A spiral galaxy has a flat disk, a central bulge and winding arms.
items.d: Its arms often contain gas, dust and young stars.

items.t: An elliptical galaxy looks round or oval.
items.d: It usually has less cool gas and dust than a spiral galaxy.

items.t: An irregular galaxy has no simple spiral or oval shape.
items.d: Gravity from nearby galaxies can help distort its form.

items.t: The Milky Way belongs to a group of galaxies called the Local Group.
items.d: The group includes the Andromeda Galaxy and dozens of smaller galaxies.

items.t: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away.
items.d: Under a dark sky, it can be seen without a telescope as a faint smudge.

items.t: The center of the Milky Way lies toward the constellation Sagittarius.
items.d: Thick dust clouds hide much of it from visible-light telescopes.

items.t: Infrared and radio waves can pass through some space dust.
items.d: They help astronomers study regions hidden from visible light.

items.t: A supermassive black hole sits at the center of the Milky Way.
items.d: It is called Sagittarius A* and has about four million Suns of mass.

items.t: Galaxies gather into groups and clusters because of gravity.
items.d: Clusters can contain hundreds or thousands of galaxies.

items.t: The universe is expanding.
items.d: On very large scales, the space between distant galaxy groups grows.

items.t: Light from many distant galaxies is shifted toward redder wavelengths.
items.d: This redshift helps show that the universe is expanding.

items.t: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
items.d: Astronomers estimate this using expansion and ancient light.

items.t: The cosmic microwave background is faint light from the early universe.
items.d: It now reaches us mostly as microwaves from every direction.

items.t: A quasar is a brilliant center of a distant galaxy.
items.d: Gas falling toward a supermassive black hole releases enormous energy.

items.t: An asteroid is a rocky or metallic object that orbits the Sun.
items.d: Asteroids are much smaller than planets.

items.t: Most known asteroids orbit in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.
items.d: Jupiter's gravity helped stop them from joining into one planet.

items.t: Asteroids in the main belt are usually far apart.
items.d: A spacecraft can cross the belt without weaving through crowded rocks.

items.t: A comet has a nucleus made of ice, dust and rock.
items.d: Its frozen materials warm as the comet approaches the Sun.

items.t: A comet can grow a glowing cloud and tails near the Sun.
items.d: The cloud around its nucleus is called a coma.

items.t: A comet's tails point mostly away from the Sun.
items.d: Sunlight and the solar wind push material outward.

items.t: A comet may have a curved dust tail and a straighter ion tail.
items.d: The two tails respond differently to sunlight and the solar wind.

items.t: Many comets travel around the Sun on long, stretched orbits.
items.d: Some return after a few years, while others take centuries.

items.t: A meteoroid is a small natural rock or metal object in space.
items.d: Many are fragments of asteroids or comets.

items.t: A meteor is the streak of light made by a meteoroid entering our atmosphere.
items.d: Air heats the object and the gas around it until they glow.

items.t: A meteorite is a piece of space rock that reaches the ground.
items.d: It is what remains after passing through the atmosphere.

items.t: Meteor showers often happen when Earth crosses a comet's dusty trail.
items.d: Many tiny particles enter the atmosphere during the same nights each year.

items.t: Meteors in a shower seem to spread from one point in the sky.
items.d: This is a perspective effect, like parallel tracks seeming to meet far away.

items.t: A refracting telescope gathers and focuses light with lenses.
items.d: Its main lens sits at the front of the telescope tube.

items.t: A reflecting telescope gathers and focuses light with mirrors.
items.d: Many large research telescopes use curved mirrors.

items.t: A telescope's aperture is the width of its main lens or mirror.
items.d: A wider aperture collects more light and reveals fainter objects.

items.t: A larger telescope can separate finer details than a smaller one.
items.d: This ability is called resolution.

items.t: Radio telescopes detect radio waves from space.
items.d: They can use large dishes or groups of antennas working together.

items.t: Space telescopes observe above Earth's atmosphere.
items.d: They avoid clouds and the atmosphere's blurring of starlight.

items.t: Adaptive optics helps ground telescopes correct atmospheric blur.
items.d: A mirror changes shape rapidly to sharpen the view.

items.t: Binoculars can reveal more night-sky objects than unaided eyes.
items.d: They gather extra light and show a wide area of sky.

items.t: Eyes need time to adjust to darkness.
items.d: After about 20 to 30 minutes, faint stars can become easier to see.

items.t: The Sun is a star.
items.d: It looks much bigger than other stars because it is much closer to Earth.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: In empty space, light travels about 300,000 kilometers in one second.

items.t: Earth takes about a year to go around the Sun.
items.d: Earth spins as it travels, so different places get daylight at different times.

items.t: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight.
items.d: As the Moon goes around Earth, we see different amounts of its sunny side.

items.t: The Moon spins once in about the same time it takes to go around Earth.
items.d: That is why we see nearly the same side of the Moon from Earth all the time.

items.t: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks some of the Sun's light from reaching Earth.
items.d: People in the Moon's shadow can see the Sun partly or fully covered.

items.t: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.
items.d: It takes about 88 Earth days to go around the Sun once.

items.t: Venus takes longer to spin once than it takes to go around the Sun.
items.d: One spin takes about 243 Earth days. One trip around the Sun takes about 225.

items.t: Mars owes much of its red color to rusty dust.
items.d: Some of the iron in its rocks and dust has reacted with oxygen, like rust on an old bike.

items.t: Mars has two small moons.
items.d: Their names are Phobos and Deimos.

items.t: Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system.
