items.d: The Great Red Spot you can see in pictures of Jupiter is a huge storm.

items.t: Saturn's rings are made mostly of pieces of ice.
items.d: The pieces stay in motion, circling Saturn.

items.t: Uranus spins almost on its side.
items.d: Picture a spinning top that keeps spinning while tipped almost all the way over.

items.t: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to circle the Sun.
items.d: It is the farthest of the eight planets from the Sun.

items.t: We live in a galaxy called the Milky Way.
items.d: A galaxy is a huge group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.

items.t: The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
items.d: Earth is the third planet in that line.

items.t: Our solar system is the Sun and everything that travels around it.
items.d: That includes eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and icy objects.

items.t: The Sun and the planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
items.d: They grew inside a spinning cloud of gas and dust.

items.t: Earth's average distance from the Sun is about 150 million kilometers.
items.d: Nonstop at 100 kilometers per hour, the drive would take more than 170 years.

items.t: If the Sun were a basketball, Earth would be a tiny seed about 25 meters away.
items.d: On this model, the Moon is a speck about 7 centimeters from Earth.

items.t: The four planets closest to the Sun are rocky worlds.
items.d: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars all have solid ground.

items.t: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giant planets.
items.d: They are much bigger than Earth and have no solid ground to stand on.

items.t: Jupiter and Saturn are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
items.d: These light gases are the main ingredients of those two giant planets.

items.t: The Sun holds more than 99 percent of the solar system's material.
items.d: All the planets and moons together are only a small share.

items.t: So far, Earth is the only place we know that has life.
items.d: Spacecraft look for water and chemical clues, but they have not found living things elsewhere.

items.t: About 109 Earths could fit side by side across the Sun.
items.d: The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometers across.

items.t: The Sun has about 1.3 million times Earth's volume.
items.d: Volume tells how much space something takes up.

items.t: Deep in the Sun, hydrogen nuclei join to form helium and release energy.
items.d: That energy eventually reaches us as light and heat.

items.t: The Sun's surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius.
items.d: The core is far hotter, about 15 million degrees Celsius.

items.t: Sunspots are darker patches on the Sun.
items.d: They are cooler patches linked to the Sun's magnetism, but they are still very hot.

items.t: The Sun blows a stream of particles called the solar wind.
items.d: These particles stream far past the planets. Some help create auroras on Earth.

items.t: Earth's seasons happen because the planet is tilted.
items.d: The tilt is about 23.5 degrees. The half leaning toward the Sun has summer.

items.t: Earth is closest to the Sun in January.
items.d: It is farthest in July. The difference is small and does not cause the seasons.

items.t: Earth has a magnetic field that reaches far into space.
items.d: Compass needles line up with it. It also guides many particles from the Sun.

items.t: Auroras are colorful lights in the sky near Earth's poles.
items.d: They appear when particles from space hit gases high in the air. Green is the most common color.

items.t: From space, Earth looks mostly blue, with white clouds.
items.d: Oceans cover most of the surface, and clouds swirl above green and brown land.

items.t: Some Mars rovers were lowered by a rocket platform.
items.d: After a parachute slowed them, the platform hovered and set the rover down on cables.

items.t: Mercury is the smallest of the eight planets.
items.d: It is about 40 percent wider than Earth's Moon.

items.t: From sunrise to sunrise on Mercury takes about 176 Earth days.
items.d: Daylight lasts about 88 Earth days, then night lasts about 88 more.

items.t: Mercury has almost no air to hold in heat.
items.d: Daytime can reach about 430 degrees Celsius. Night can drop to about minus 180.

items.t: Some deep craters at Mercury's poles hold water ice.
items.d: Their floors never get sunlight, so the ice can stay frozen.

items.t: Venus is almost the same size as Earth.
items.d: It is only a little smaller, but a thick blanket of air makes it very different.

items.t: Venus is the hottest planet, hotter even than Mercury.
items.d: Thick carbon dioxide air traps heat. The surface is about 460 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Air pressure on Venus is about 90 times the pressure on Earth.
items.d: The air is so heavy that a spacecraft needs to be very strong to work there.

items.t: Venus spins in the opposite direction from Earth.
items.d: Because of that backward spin, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

items.t: Venus is the brightest planet in our sky.
items.d: People call it the Morning Star or the Evening Star, but it is a planet, not a star.

items.t: Thick clouds hide the rocky surface of Venus.
items.d: Spacecraft used radar, which can see through clouds, to map the ground.

items.t: Mars takes about 687 Earth days to go around the Sun.
items.d: One Earth year is about 365 days, so Mars takes almost two Earth years.

items.t: A day on Mars is only a little longer than a day on Earth.
items.d: It lasts about 24 hours and 37 minutes.

items.t: Mars has a thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.
items.d: Its pressure is under one hundredth of Earth's, far too thin to breathe.

items.t: Mars is usually very cold.
items.d: A typical temperature is about minus 60 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Gravity on Mars is about 38 percent as strong as on Earth.
items.d: An object would feel about 38 percent as heavy on Mars as it does on Earth.

items.t: Mars has ice caps at both poles.
items.d: They contain frozen water and frozen carbon dioxide, also called dry ice.

items.t: Mars has dry riverbeds and old lake bottoms.
items.d: They show that liquid water flowed there a long time ago.

items.t: Dust storms on Mars can grow huge.
items.d: Some spread across much of the planet and hide the surface for weeks.

items.t: Sunsets on Mars can look blue.
items.d: Fine dust scatters light so the glow around the setting Sun looks blue.

items.t: The biggest volcano in the solar system is on Mars.
items.d: Olympus Mons is more than twice as tall as Mount Everest and hundreds of kilometers wide.

items.t: Mars has a canyon system thousands of kilometers long.
items.d: Valles Marineris is about 4,000 kilometers long, far longer than the Grand Canyon.

items.t: Phobos races around Mars in about 8 hours.
items.d: It moves so fast that, from Mars, it rises in the west and sets in the east.

items.t: Jupiter spins so fast that its day lasts about 10 hours.
items.d: The quick spin makes Jupiter a little wider around the middle than from top to bottom.

items.t: Jupiter's stripes are bands of clouds.
items.d: Neighboring bands blow in opposite directions in very strong winds.

items.t: At Jupiter's cloud tops, gravity is about 2.5 times Earth's.
items.d: An object there would feel about 2.5 times as heavy as it does on Earth.

items.t: Jupiter's four biggest moons were discovered in 1610.
items.d: Galileo Galilei found Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto with a telescope.

items.t: Ganymede is the biggest moon in the solar system.
items.d: This moon of Jupiter is wider than the planet Mercury.

items.t: Two Voyager spacecraft left Earth in 1977 to visit the giant planets.
items.d: Each one carries a disk of sounds and pictures, a greeting from Earth.

items.t: Io, a moon of Jupiter, has many active volcanoes.
items.d: Jupiter's gravity squeezes Io as it orbits, heating the inside until rock melts.

items.t: Europa's surface is a cracked shell of ice.
items.d: The cracks and magnetic clues are strong signs of a salty ocean under the ice.

items.t: Saturn's average density is less than the density of water.
items.d: Its average density is about 70 percent of water's.

items.t: Saturn's rings are very wide but amazingly thin.
items.d: They stretch tens of thousands of kilometers, yet many parts are only about 10 meters thick.

items.t: A giant six-sided cloud pattern surrounds Saturn's north pole.
items.d: Strong winds around the pole help form this unusual shape.

items.t: Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
items.d: Its air is mostly nitrogen. It is so cold that methane, a gas on Earth, forms lakes.

items.t: Enceladus shoots jets of water ice into space.
items.d: A spacecraft flew through the spray and found water vapor and ice grains.

items.t: A probe named Huygens landed on Titan in 2005.
items.d: It touched down on Saturn's largest moon and sent photos back from the surface.

items.t: Uranus takes about 84 Earth years to orbit the Sun.
items.d: One year on Uranus lasts about as long as 84 years on Earth.

items.t: Methane gas makes Uranus and Neptune look blue.
items.d: Methane soaks up red light, so the light that bounces back looks blue or blue-green.

items.t: Neptune has some of the fastest winds in the solar system.
items.d: Those winds can blow at more than 1,000 kilometers per hour.

items.t: Triton orbits Neptune backward.
items.d: It circles opposite Neptune's spin. Its surface is colder than minus 200 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Pluto is a dwarf planet, smaller than Earth's Moon.
items.d: It usually orbits beyond Neptune. It shares that icy region with many other objects.

items.t: Pluto takes about 248 Earth years to go around the Sun.
items.d: Earth goes around the Sun 248 times while Pluto goes around once.

items.t: Pluto has five known moons.
items.d: The biggest, Charon, is so large that they both orbit a point in the space between them.

items.t: A spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015.
items.d: New Horizons saw icy mountains, a bright heart-shaped region and a plain of nitrogen ice.

items.t: Ceres is a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.
items.d: It orbits between Mars and Jupiter and is the largest object there.

items.t: The asteroid belt is mostly empty space.
items.d: The rocks are far apart. Together they hold much less material than the Moon.

items.t: Some asteroids share Jupiter's path around the Sun.
items.d: Called Trojans, they travel in groups ahead of Jupiter and behind it.

items.t: Spacecraft have brought pieces of asteroids back to Earth.
items.d: Scientists study those old rocks to learn what the planets formed from.

items.t: The Moon is about 384,000 kilometers from Earth.
items.d: At 100 kilometers per hour, nonstop, the trip would take about 160 days.

items.t: The Moon is about one quarter as wide as Earth.
items.d: Earth is about 13,000 kilometers across, and the Moon is about 3,500.

items.t: Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth as strong as on Earth.
items.d: An object would feel about one sixth as heavy on the Moon as it does on Earth.

items.t: The Moon has almost no air.
items.d: Without air, there is nothing to breathe, so astronauts carry oxygen in their suits.

items.t: Daylight on the Moon lasts about two weeks.
items.d: Night lasts about two weeks too. A full day there is about as long as a month on Earth.

items.t: The far side of the Moon is not always dark.
items.d: It gets two weeks of sunshine, just like the side that faces Earth. We just cannot see it from here.

items.t: The dark patches on the Moon are plains of old lava.
items.d: Long ago people thought they were seas. They are really dry rock.

items.t: Footprints on the Moon can last a very long time.
items.d: There is no wind or rain to erase them.

items.t: Water ice sits in shadowed craters near the Moon's poles.
items.d: The Sun never shines on those floors, so the ice stays frozen.

items.t: The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth.
items.d: It drifts about 4 centimeters farther each year. Mirrors left on the Moon help measure this.

items.t: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth blocks sunlight from the Moon.
items.d: The Moon can look reddish because Earth's air bends some red light into the shadow.

items.t: From the Moon's near side, Earth looks big and bright.
items.d: Earth is wider than the Moon, and its clouds reflect a lot of sunlight.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin was the first person to orbit Earth.
items.d: He flew on April 12, 1961. His trip around the planet took about 108 minutes.

items.t: Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space.
items.d: She orbited Earth in 1963, flying for almost three days.

items.t: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.
items.d: The Apollo 11 landing was in July 1969. Buzz Aldrin stepped out soon after Armstrong.

items.t: Twelve Apollo astronauts walked on the Moon.
items.d: Six landings between 1969 and 1972 each had two people walk on the surface.

items.t: Apollo crews brought about 380 kilograms of Moon rocks to Earth.
items.d: Labs on Earth still study those rocks to learn what the Moon is made of.

items.t: Apollo crews took about three days to reach the Moon.
items.d: Then a small lander flew down while the main ship stayed in orbit around the Moon.

items.t: The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometers up.
items.d: It goes around Earth about once every 90 minutes.

items.t: The space station travels at about 28,000 kilometers per hour.
items.d: Crews see about 16 sunrises during a single day on Earth.

items.t: Astronauts float because they are falling around Earth.
items.d: Gravity still pulls. They fall together with the station, so their feet do not press down.

items.t: Astronauts exercise for about two hours each day in orbit.
items.d: Their bodies do less work against gravity, so exercise keeps muscles and bones strong.

items.t: In orbit, water forms round floating blobs.
items.d: Because it is falling with the station, it is not pulled flat. It clings together as a ball.

items.t: The sky looks black in space even when the Sun is out.
items.d: There is no air to scatter sunlight. On Earth, that scattering makes the sky blue.

items.t: A rocket moves forward by pushing gas out the back.
items.d: The gas pushes back on the rocket just as hard, and that push lifts it.

items.t: Most of a rocket at liftoff is propellant.
items.d: Propellant includes fuel and an oxidizer. Empty tanks and used stages drop away during flight.

items.t: Many rockets head east to get a boost from Earth's spin.
items.d: The ground itself is moving east, fastest near the equator.

items.t: A returning crew capsule uses a heat shield, then parachutes.
items.d: The shield takes the heat of rushing into the air. Parachutes slow the final fall.

items.t: A small helicopter named Ingenuity flew on Mars.
items.d: In 2021 it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. Its blades spun fast in the thin air.

items.t: Penguins use their wings like flippers.
items.d: They flap them underwater to swim after food.

items.t: American flamingos get their pink color from their food.
items.d: Tiny algae and small animals they eat contain pigments, which give their feathers color.

items.t: Bats are the only mammals that can fly by flapping their wings.
items.d: Flying squirrels glide, like a paper plane.

items.t: Dolphins come to the surface for air.
items.d: They breathe through a blowhole on top of the head.

items.t: Male humpback whales sing long songs.
items.d: Their songs repeat groups of sounds and can be heard underwater.

items.t: An elephant uses its trunk to pick up food.
items.d: Its trunk is a long nose that can grab a meal and carry it to its mouth.

items.t: A butterfly starts life as an egg.
items.d: It hatches as a caterpillar, then changes inside a chrysalis before coming out as a butterfly.

items.t: Spiders have eight legs. Insects have six.
items.d: A ladybug may look a bit like a tiny spider, but it has six legs.

items.t: Female sea turtles lay their eggs on land.
items.d: They dig a nest in the sand and cover the eggs before going back to sea.

items.t: A kangaroo joey finishes much of its early growth in a pouch.
items.d: The newborn climbs into its mother's pouch, where it drinks milk.

items.t: Crocodiles lay eggs and can guard their nests.
items.d: A mother crocodile may even carry her hatchlings to water in her mouth.

items.t: Beavers build dams from sticks, mud and other things they find.
items.d: A dam slows a stream and can make a pond behind it.

items.t: An ostrich can run fast, but it cannot fly.
items.d: It has long, strong legs that help it take big steps.

items.t: A male seahorse carries the young before they are born.
items.d: The female puts her eggs into a pouch on the male. The young grow there until he gives birth.

items.t: Polar bears have black skin under their fur.
items.d: Their fur looks white, which helps them blend in with snow and ice.

items.t: A giraffe has seven neck bones, the same number as you.
items.d: Those bones are very long, which lets the neck reach high leaves.

items.t: A blue whale is the biggest animal alive today.
items.d: The biggest ones can grow to about 30 meters long.

items.t: Whales and dolphins move their tails up and down.
items.d: Most fish swim by swinging their tails from side to side.

items.t: A whale mother feeds her baby milk.
items.d: Whales are mammals, so babies drink milk even though they live in the sea.

items.t: Hippos are the closest living relatives of whales.
items.d: Hippos are nearer cousins to whales than to pigs or horses.

items.t: A bat's wing is a hand with very long fingers.
items.d: Skin stretched between the fingers makes the wing.

items.t: Bats are not blind. Many find their way by echoes.
items.d: The bat makes clicks and listens for the sounds that bounce back.

items.t: A camel's hump stores fat, not water.
items.d: The fat is stored energy. A camel still has to drink when it can.

items.t: A dromedary camel has one hump. A Bactrian camel has two.
items.d: Both can live in dry places and travel far between drinks of water.

items.t: A camel can close its nostrils to keep out blowing sand.
items.d: Long eyelashes help keep sand out of its eyes too.

items.t: A koala is not a bear. It lives mostly in trees.
items.d: It eats eucalyptus leaves and sleeps for most of the day.

items.t: A giant panda is a bear that eats mostly bamboo.
items.d: A special wrist bone works like a thumb and helps it grip the stalks.

items.t: The elephant is the largest living animal on land.
items.d: Even a baby elephant can weigh about 100 kilograms.

items.t: An elephant's tusks are very long teeth.
items.d: Elephants use them to dig, to lift things, and to strip bark.

items.t: A rhino's horn is made of keratin, like your hair and nails.
items.d: The horn grows from the skin. It is not made of bone.

items.t: A hippo's eyes, ears, and nose sit on top of its head.
items.d: It can rest almost underwater and still see, hear, and breathe.

items.t: Every zebra has its own stripe pattern.
items.d: No two zebras match exactly, a bit like human fingerprints.

items.t: The cheetah is the fastest animal on land.
items.d: A long tail helps it balance when it turns at high speed.

items.t: Lions live together in family groups called prides.
items.d: Females in the pride rest together and help care for the cubs.

items.t: Polar bears live in the Arctic, not in Antarctica.
items.d: Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere, so they never meet polar bears in the wild.

items.t: Chimpanzees use sticks as tools.
items.d: A chimp pokes a stick into a mound so termites climb on, then eats them.

items.t: Apes do not have tails. Most monkeys do.
items.d: Gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans, gibbons, and people are apes.

items.t: A platypus is a mammal that lays eggs.
items.d: Its bill can sense tiny electric signals from animals in the water.

items.t: A kangaroo uses its tail like an extra leg.
items.d: When it walks slowly, it plants the tail and swings both hind legs forward.

items.t: Sloths hang upside down in trees for much of their lives.
items.d: Algae can grow in their fur and give the coat a green tint.

items.t: A sea otter can use a rock as a tool.
items.d: Floating on its back, it opens hard shells against a rock on its chest.

items.t: Sea lions have small ear flaps. True seals do not.
items.d: Sea lions can walk on land by turning their back flippers forward.

items.t: Orcas are dolphins, and they are the biggest ones.
items.d: They live in family groups and keep in touch with clicks and calls.

items.t: Dolphins find things by listening to echoes.
items.d: They make clicks, and the echoes tell them the shape and distance of objects.

items.t: Rabbits are not rodents, even though they look a bit like them.
items.d: Behind their two big front teeth is a second small pair. Rodents do not have those.

items.t: Hummingbirds can hover in place and fly backward.
items.d: Their wings beat so fast that they look like a blur.

items.t: Owls can turn their heads very far, but not all the way around.
items.d: Their eyes stay fixed in place, so the head does the turning.

items.t: An owl's feathers help it fly almost without a sound.
items.d: Soft, fringed edges break up the noise that wings usually make.

items.t: A father emperor penguin keeps the egg on his feet.
items.d: A warm fold of belly skin covers the egg for about two months.

items.t: The ostrich is the largest bird alive today.
items.d: An ostrich egg is also the largest egg of any living bird.

items.t: Ostriches do not bury their heads in the sand.
items.d: A low head usually means the bird is feeding or tending its eggs.

items.t: The bend you see in a flamingo's leg is its ankle.
items.d: The real knee is hidden high up near the body, under the feathers.

items.t: A pelican's pouch is a scoop, not a bag for saving fish.
items.d: It scoops up water and fish, drains the water, and swallows the fish.

items.t: Arctic terns travel from the Arctic to the Antarctic each year.
items.d: That round trip is one of the longest yearly journeys any animal makes.

items.t: Many geese fly together in a V shape.
items.d: Flying just behind and to the side lets a goose save energy.

items.t: Ducks rub oil on their feathers to help stay waterproof.
items.d: The oil comes from a gland near the tail, and the duck spreads it with its bill.

items.t: A parrot can copy sounds, including people's words.
items.d: Being able to copy a word does not mean the bird understands it.

items.t: Many flying birds have hollow bones.
items.d: Air spaces inside the bones keep the skeleton light for flying.

items.t: A puffin can carry several fish in its bill at one time.
items.d: Small spines in the mouth hold the fish while the puffin catches more.

items.t: A kiwi has nostrils on the tip of its beak.
items.d: It smells for worms in the soil. Kiwis live in New Zealand and cannot fly.

items.t: Weaver birds build nests by weaving grass.
items.d: In many kinds, the male weaves a hanging nest and leaves a small doorway.

items.t: A duckling follows its mother soon after it hatches.
items.d: This fast learning is called imprinting. It helps the duckling stay with its parent.

items.t: A male peacock spreads a giant fan of feathers.
items.d: He shows off for the female, called a peahen, who is mostly brown.

items.t: Honeybees dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
items.d: The direction of the dance shows the way, and dancing longer means the flowers are farther.

items.t: Honeybees store honey in six-sided wax cells.
items.d: Those six-sided shapes fit together tightly, with no gaps between them.

items.t: Butterflies can taste with their feet.
items.d: Landing on a leaf tells the butterfly if it is a good place for eggs.

items.t: Tiny scales cover a butterfly's wings.
items.d: The scales make the colors and patterns you see on the wings.

items.t: Ants lay down scent trails for the colony to follow.
items.d: That is how a line of ants can lead straight to a dropped crumb.

items.t: Leafcutter ants farm a fungus for food.
items.d: They carry leaf pieces home, and the fungus grows on the leaves.

items.t: A housefly has just one pair of wings.
items.d: Where a second pair would be, tiny knobs help the fly balance in the air.

items.t: A firefly's light comes from a chemical glow.
items.d: The light stays cool. Flashing fireflies use patterns to signal their own kind.

items.t: Crickets chirp faster on warmer nights.
items.d: Warmer air speeds up their wing muscles, so the chirps come faster.

items.t: Water striders walk on the surface of a pond.
items.d: Hair on their feet keeps them from breaking through the water's surface.

items.t: A ladybug's hard wing covers protect its thin flying wings.
items.d: The covers lift up, and the thin wings unfold when the ladybug flies.

items.t: A dragonfly can beat its front and back wings separately.
items.d: That lets it hover, turn fast, and even fly backward.

items.t: Not every spider builds a web to catch food.
items.d: A jumping spider sneaks close, then leaps onto a small insect.

items.t: A pill bug is related to crabs, not to insects.
items.d: It wears its skeleton outside and can roll into a tight ball.

items.t: A chameleon can look two ways at the same time.
items.d: Each eye swivels on its own, so one may look forward and one back.

items.t: A chameleon's colors change with mood, light, and heat.
items.d: They do not simply copy the color of whatever they are sitting on.

items.t: Many geckos can walk straight up a smooth wall.
items.d: Tiny hairs on their toes grip the wall, even on glass.

items.t: Snakes smell by flicking their tongues.
items.d: The tongue picks up scents and passes them to an organ in the mouth.

items.t: A snake can open its mouth far wider than its head looks.
items.d: The two halves of the lower jaw can spread apart and are joined by stretchy tissue.

items.t: A turtle cannot crawl out of its shell.
items.d: The shell is part of the skeleton, with ribs and backbone inside it.

items.t: A tortoise is a kind of turtle that lives on land.
items.d: Tortoises walk on sturdy feet. Sea turtles swim with flippers.

items.t: Most frogs can breathe through their skin and their lungs.
items.d: Their skin has to stay damp for the oxygen to pass through.

items.t: A tadpole slowly changes into a frog.
items.d: It begins with gills and a tail, then grows legs and lungs.

items.t: Crocodiles are more closely related to birds than to lizards.
items.d: Their family line split from lizards long before it split from the dinosaur line.

items.t: A shark's skeleton is cartilage, not bone.
items.d: Cartilage is tough and bendy, like the material in your outer ear.

items.t: The whale shark is the largest fish in the world.
items.d: It swims with its mouth open and filters tiny food from the water.

items.t: Sharks grow new teeth for their whole lives.
items.d: The teeth sit in rows. A back tooth moves up when a front one falls out.

items.t: Sharks can detect weak electricity in the water.
items.d: Sensors on the snout help them notice animals close by.

items.t: Most fish feel ripples through a line of sensors on each side.
items.d: It helps a fish notice other animals moving nearby, even in cloudy water.

items.t: A seahorse is a fish, and it swims upright.
items.d: It can wrap its curly tail around seaweed to stay in place.

items.t: Clownfish can live safely in a sea anemone's tentacles.
items.d: A special coating on their skin protects them from the stings.

items.t: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
items.d: Two hearts serve the gills. The third heart serves the rest of the body.

items.t: An octopus has no bones in its body.
items.d: That is why it can slip through a hole barely wider than its beak.

items.t: An octopus can change color to blend in with the sea floor.
items.d: It can also raise bumps on its skin to look like rocks or coral.

items.t: A cuttlefish can change color in the blink of an eye.
items.d: Small color sacs in the skin open and close to make new patterns.

items.t: A squid has eight arms and two long tentacles.
items.d: To move quickly, it shoots a jet of water out behind it.

items.t: A sea star is not a fish, even though some call it a starfish.
items.d: It has no backbone and creeps along on many tiny tube feet.

items.t: A jellyfish has no brain, no heart, and no bones.
items.d: A spread-out net of nerves helps it move through the water.

items.t: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called coral polyps.
items.d: Each polyp builds a hard little cup. Over many years, the cups can build a reef.

items.t: A hermit crab makes its home in an empty shell.
items.d: As it grows, it leaves the old shell and moves into a bigger one.

items.t: An adult flounder has both eyes on one side of its head.
items.d: A baby flounder starts with one eye on each side, and one eye moves.

items.t: Barnacles are relatives of crabs, even though they look like shells.
items.d: A barnacle sticks to a rock and waves feathery legs to catch food.

items.t: A scallop has many small eyes around the edge of its shell.
items.d: Those eyes spot changes in light, so the scallop can clap its shell and swim away.

items.t: An oyster can grow a pearl inside its shell.
items.d: If something bothers it inside, the oyster coats that bit with smooth shell.

items.t: Many salmon swim back to the stream where they were born.
items.d: They can follow the smell of their home water on the long trip back from the sea.

items.t: A goldfish can remember things for months.
items.d: The story that a goldfish forgets everything in seconds is not true.

items.t: A pufferfish swallows water to puff itself into a ball.
items.d: The round shape makes the fish much harder to swallow.

items.t: Parrotfish help make the white sand on some coral beaches.
items.d: They crunch coral as they eat, and the ground-up pieces come out later as sand.

items.t: An electric eel is a fish that makes its own electricity.
items.d: Pulses of electricity help it find food in dark, muddy rivers.

items.t: An adult sponge is an animal that usually stays fixed in one spot.
items.d: Water flows through its body, and it strains out tiny bits of food.

items.t: Your smallest bones are inside your ears.
items.d: These tiny bones help pass vibrations from your eardrum to the inner ear.

items.t: Your pupil is the opening in the middle of your eye.
items.d: It usually gets bigger in dim light to let more light in.

items.t: Your heart is a pump made of muscle.
items.d: Every beat pushes blood through your body.

items.t: When you breathe in, oxygen from the air can pass into your blood.
items.d: It passes through the walls of tiny air sacs in your lungs.

items.t: Your tongue and nose work together when you taste food.
items.d: When you have a stuffy nose, food may seem to have less flavor.

items.t: The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of Earth.
items.d: It divides Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

items.t: The Pacific Ocean is Earth's largest ocean.
items.d: It lies between Asia and Australia on one side and the Americas on the other.

items.t: The South Pole sits in Antarctica.
items.d: At the South Pole, a thick sheet of ice covers the land.

items.t: A map scale helps you work out real distances.
items.d: If 1 centimeter on a map stands for 1 kilometer, 3 centimeters stand for 3 kilometers.

items.t: An island is a piece of land surrounded by water.
items.d: An island can sit in a lake or river as well as in the ocean.

items.t: Word of the day: nocturnal.
items.d: A nocturnal animal is active at night. A barn owl often hunts after dark.

items.t: Word of the day: peninsula.
items.d: A peninsula is land with water around most of it. Much of Florida sits between the Gulf and the Atlantic Ocean.

items.t: Word of the day: palindrome.
items.d: A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. Try it with the word level.

items.t: Word of the day: transparent.
items.d: If something is transparent, you can see clearly through it, like through clean window glass.

items.t: Word of the day: migrate.
items.d: To migrate is to move from one place to another. Many birds do this as the seasons change.

items.t: A grown-up's skeleton has 206 bones.
items.d: Babies are born with more bones. Some of those bones join as the child grows.

items.t: Children usually have 20 baby teeth.
items.d: Baby teeth later fall out so larger adult teeth can take their places.

items.t: People can grow up to 32 adult teeth.
items.d: That count includes wisdom teeth, which do not grow in for everyone.

items.t: Tooth enamel is the hardest material in the human body.
items.d: Enamel is the tough outer layer of the part of a tooth you see.

items.t: Each of your hands has 27 bones.
items.d: The hands and feet together hold more than half of a grown-up's bones.

items.t: The femur is the longest bone in the human body.
items.d: The femur is your thigh bone. It helps you stand, walk, and run.

items.t: Your outer ears and nose tip are mostly cartilage.
items.d: Cartilage is bendier than bone, but it still holds a shape.

items.t: The left lung is a little smaller than the right lung.
items.d: That leaves room for the heart, which sits a bit left of center.

items.t: Your body temperature is usually about 37 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is about 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

items.t: More than half of your body is water.
items.d: Water is in your blood, your muscles, and even your bones.

items.t: Your skin is your body's largest organ.
items.d: It helps hold water in, keeps out germs, and lets you feel touch.

items.t: Your body has about 600 skeletal muscles, and many move your bones.
items.d: A muscle can pull on a bone, but it cannot push.

items.t: Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
items.d: Those tiny skin ridges form before birth and stay with you for life.

items.t: You can taste sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami.
items.d: Umami is a savory taste, like the taste in a ripe tomato.

items.t: Word of the day: archipelago.
items.d: An archipelago is a group of islands. Hawaii is one in the Pacific.

items.t: Word of the day: delta.
items.d: A delta is low land a river builds at its mouth. The Nile has a big delta.

items.t: Word of the day: tributary.
items.d: A tributary flows into a larger river. The Missouri flows into the Mississippi.

items.t: Word of the day: humidity.
items.d: Humidity is how much water vapor is in the air. High humidity can make a warm day feel sticky.

items.t: Word of the day: glacier.
items.d: A glacier is a thick mass of ice that slowly flows. It can carve a valley as it moves.

items.t: Word of the day: erosion.
items.d: Erosion wears away rock and soil. Rain and rivers can carry the bits elsewhere.

items.t: Word of the day: oasis.
items.d: An oasis is a place in a desert where water lets plants grow.

items.t: Word of the day: strait.
items.d: A strait is a narrow waterway between two larger bodies of water. The Strait of Gibraltar is one.

items.t: Word of the day: isthmus.
items.d: An isthmus is a narrow strip of land joining two larger areas. The Isthmus of Panama is one.

items.t: Word of the day: precipitation.
items.d: Precipitation is water falling from the sky. Rain, snow, and hail all count.

items.t: Word of the day: climate.
items.d: Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. Deserts have a dry climate.

items.t: Word of the day: pollen.
items.d: Pollen is a powder that helps flowering plants make seeds. Bees often carry it from bloom to bloom.

items.t: Word of the day: germinate.
items.d: A seed germinates when it starts to grow. Warmth and water help a bean germinate.

items.t: Word of the day: fossil.
items.d: A fossil is preserved evidence of ancient life, such as a bone, shell, footprint, or leaf print.

items.t: Word of the day: homophone.
items.d: Homophones sound alike but mean different things. See and sea are homophones.

items.t: Asia is the largest continent.
items.d: From Saudi Arabia to India, China, and Japan, those lands are part of Asia.

items.t: Australia is the smallest of the seven continents.
items.d: Australia is also one country. Europe is the next smallest continent.

items.t: Africa is the only continent in all four hemispheres.
items.d: The equator and the 0 degrees longitude line both cross it, so it reaches north, south, east, and west.

items.t: Greenland is the world's largest island.
items.d: Australia is larger, but maps count it as a continent, not an island.

items.t: The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth.
items.d: It stretches across North Africa, from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea.

items.t: Antarctica is a cold desert.
items.d: So little new snow or rain falls each year that it counts as a desert.

items.t: The Amazon River carries more water than any other river.
items.d: It flows east across South America into the Atlantic Ocean.

items.t: The Nile River flows north to the Mediterranean Sea.
items.d: It crosses northeastern Africa and runs through Egypt.

items.t: Mount Everest is Earth's highest peak above sea level.
items.d: The top is about 8,849 meters above sea level, in the Himalayas.

items.t: The Andes are the longest mountain chain on land.
items.d: They run about 7,000 kilometers down the west side of South America.

items.t: The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon.
items.d: Over a very long time, it cut down through layers of rock in Arizona.

items.t: A fjord is a deep, narrow arm of the sea.
items.d: Glaciers carved many fjords long ago. Later the sea filled them.

items.t: The country of Ecuador is named for the equator.
items.d: The equator crosses the country, which is in South America.

items.t: Canberra is the capital of Australia.
items.d: Sydney has more people, but the capital city is Canberra.

items.t: Japan is made up of thousands of islands.
items.d: Most people live on Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, or Shikoku.

items.t: Huge plates of rock under the land and sea creep very slowly.
items.d: They move only a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.

items.t: Latitude tells how far north or south of the equator you are.
items.d: The equator is 0 degrees latitude. The North Pole is 90 degrees north.

items.t: Longitude tells how far east or west a place is.
items.d: Zero degrees of longitude runs through Greenwich, London. That line is the prime meridian.

items.t: Maps often show five oceans on Earth.
items.d: They are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic Oceans.

items.t: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest ocean.
items.d: It lies in the far north and surrounds the North Pole.

items.t: About 71 percent of Earth's surface is ocean.
items.d: Spin a globe and point anywhere. Your finger will often land on water.

items.t: About 97 percent of Earth's water is salty.
items.d: Fresh water in rivers, lakes, and ice is only a small share of all Earth's water.

items.t: Ocean tides are raised mainly by the Moon's gravity.
items.d: The Sun's gravity changes tides too, so some high tides are higher than others.

items.t: Most ocean waves are made by the wind.
items.d: The wind drags on the surface, and the water rises and falls.

items.t: About 90 percent of an iceberg hides underwater.
items.d: The ice floats, so only a small part shows above the sea.

items.t: The Mariana Trench is the deepest known part of the ocean.
items.d: The bottom there is about 11 kilometers below the surface.

items.t: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called polyps.
items.d: Each polyp leaves a small stony cup. Millions of cups make the reef.

items.t: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system.
items.d: It stretches more than 2,000 kilometers off Australia's northeast coast.

items.t: Earth has seasons because the planet is tilted.
items.d: When your part of Earth leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits it more directly.

items.t: Away from the equator, summer days last longer than winter days.
items.d: Earth's tilt keeps the Sun above the horizon for more hours in summer.

items.t: Heat from the Sun turns liquid water into invisible vapor.
items.d: That is evaporation. It is why wet clothes dry on a sunny line.

items.t: Clouds form when water vapor cools into tiny drops or ice.
items.d: A cold window fogs up on a chilly day for the same kind of reason.

items.t: Rain falls when drops in a cloud grow large enough.
items.d: Tiny cloud drops bump and join. When they get large, gravity pulls them down.

items.t: A rainbow appears when sunlight bends through raindrops.
items.d: To see it, keep the Sun behind you and the falling rain in front.

items.t: A fainter second rainbow shows the colors in reverse.
items.d: Its light bounces twice inside each drop, so the order of colors flips.

items.t: Snowflakes often grow with six arms.
items.d: The ice inside a snowflake builds in a six-part pattern.

items.t: You see lightning before you hear its thunder.
items.d: Light arrives almost at once. Sound takes about 3 seconds to go 1 kilometer.

items.t: Fog is a cloud resting on the ground.
items.d: Tiny water drops hang in the air and hide things that are far away.

items.t: Dew is water that collects on cool grass and leaves.
items.d: At night, vapor in the air turns to liquid on those cool surfaces.

items.t: Water boils at a lower temperature high on a mountain.
items.d: At sea level it boils at 100 degrees Celsius. Lower air pressure changes that.

items.t: Green plants make their food using sunlight, water, and air.
items.d: They take carbon dioxide from the air. This is called photosynthesis.

items.t: Leaves look green because they hold chlorophyll.
items.d: Chlorophyll catches sunlight the leaf uses to make its food.

items.t: In sunlight, green plants give off oxygen.
items.d: That oxygen mixes into the air people and animals breathe.

items.t: In autumn, many green leaves turn yellow or red.
items.d: As green chlorophyll fades, yellow shows through, and some leaves make red pigments.

items.t: A seed contains a tiny plant and a store of food.
items.d: The stored food feeds the sprout until its leaves can make food.

items.t: Roots anchor a plant and take in water from the soil.
items.d: Tiny root hairs soak up water and minerals the plant needs.

items.t: Grass can keep growing after the top is cut.
items.d: It grows from low down, near the soil, not from the tips.

items.t: In plant science, a banana counts as a berry.
items.d: It develops from one flower's ovary. Wild bananas have seeds inside their flesh.

items.t: A strawberry's tiny outside dots are little fruits.
items.d: Each little fruit, called an achene, usually holds one seed.

items.t: In plant science, a tomato is a fruit.
items.d: It grows from a flower and holds seeds, which is what makes a fruit.

items.t: A potato is a fat underground stem, not a root.
items.d: This kind of stem is a tuber. The eyes on it can sprout new plants.

items.t: Cutting an onion can make your eyes water.
items.d: The cut lets out a gas that stings, and tears wash the sting away.

items.t: Many tree trunks add one new growth ring each year.
items.d: A wide ring often means a good growing year. A thin ring can mean a hard one.

items.t: Young sunflower buds turn to follow the Sun.
items.d: Once the bloom is fully open, it usually settles facing east.

items.t: People have been writing for more than 5,000 years.
items.d: Some of the oldest marks were pictures and wedge shapes pressed in clay.

items.t: Wheels have helped move heavy loads for more than 5,000 years.
items.d: A cart with wheels rolls along. Dragging the same load is much harder.

items.t: Paper was invented in China about 2,000 years ago.
items.d: Fibers from plants were mashed with water, spread flat, and dried.

items.t: In the 1400s, Gutenberg's press printed books much faster.
items.d: Metal letters could be moved around and used again for the next page.

items.t: The core of a pencil is graphite, not lead.
items.d: Graphite is a soft form of carbon. Clay is mixed in to change the hardness.

items.t: Zero, as a number, was developed in India long ago.
items.d: That was more than 1,000 years ago. Zero lets 101 mean one hundred and one.

items.t: In Roman numerals, V stands for 5 and X stands for 10.
items.d: IV means 4, because I before V takes 1 away. VI means 6.

items.t: A leap year gives February 29 days instead of 28.
items.d: They usually come every 4 years so the calendar stays lined up with the seasons.

items.t: One day has 24 hours, and one hour has 60 minutes.
items.d: A minute has 60 seconds. So one hour has 60 times 60, or 3,600 seconds.

items.t: The earliest bicycles had no pedals.
items.d: A rider sat over two wheels and pushed along with both feet.

items.t: Food cans came along before the can opener did.
items.d: For years, people had to cut a can open with a hammer and chisel.

items.t: Louis Braille created a writing system you can read by touch.
items.d: Raised dots stand for letters, and a fingertip can feel each pattern.

items.t: A popcorn kernel pops when water inside turns to steam.
items.d: The steam builds until the shell bursts and the inside puffs up.

items.t: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.
items.d: When water freezes, it spreads out, so the same amount fills more space.

items.t: A melted candy bar led to the microwave oven.
items.d: In 1945, Percy Spencer noticed the candy melt near radar gear, then tried cooking with those waves.

items.t: In 1903 the Wright brothers flew the first controlled powered airplane.
items.d: The first flight lasted 12 seconds and traveled about 37 meters.

items.t: Hook-and-loop fasteners copy the tiny hooks on a burr.
items.d: Those hooks grab loops in fur or cloth. A Swiss inventor turned that into a fastener.
